text:
Long xyz is the ai16z of this meta.

Their goal: “make billion dollar runners” - @Natan_benish 

The same way that ai16z was home turf for the best developer tooling to build AI agents, Long xyz is home turf to the best liquidity sources for tokenized assets.

Tokenized stocks liquidity flywheel = AI agents plugin/integration flywheel

Eliza gave developers a shared runtime where actions, providers, evaluators, memory, social clients and onchain tooling could all be plugged into the same agent. Every new integration made the framework more useful for the next developer, which made the next agent easier to build.

What makes Long’s launchpad different is the pre bond (dutch auction) launch mechanic. A mechanism from the NFT days where price moves down during the auction to reduce how much of an advantage snipers get at launch. Although with the recent changes, what happens after launch is the more interesting part.

Fees from volume can be routed into a vault accumulating the underlying RWA, while fees can also systematically grow LP and mechanically reduce supply. Volume isn’t purely extractive, every trade can incrementally strengthen the market structure of the token itself.

Which is a very different design philosophy from most launchpads since success creates fees for the platform but doesn’t necessarily create a stronger token.

For a launchpad to succeed beyond more than its narrative, it needs genuinely interesting tokens which can stand on their own narrative/memetics/utility. This is why you’ll see a thousand copy cats once the originator takes off and starts a new meta.

Launchpad vamps can be convincing and shiny object syndrome makes it difficult to distinguish whether an emerging eco is genuinely coming for the throne or just another short lived rotation.

The easiest way to distinguish a meta from a rotation is breadth.

One token running can be reflexivity. Multiple unrelated tokens sustaining volume, holders and liquidity is when you start getting evidence that the underlying rails themselves have PMF.

This was also part of what separated ai16z. Eliza wasn’t dependent on a single agent use case, the same runtime could power agents that interact, query external data, retain memory, execute onchain etc.

Earlier in the week Nate hinted at enhancing the depth of all assets across the platform: https://t.co/Wcf2ai5ML6

Assuming there’s some type of stocks -> AI -> NVDA routing, you’re effectively creating a liquidity graph where child markets can share a common intermediary instead of every pair needing to support completely isolated depth.

This matters as liquidity fragmentation is one of the biggest problems once you move from trench sized positions into actual size. Early on you care about asymmetric entry and incentives. Later on you care whether you can put 6-7 figs through a route without nuking yourself on price impact.

This is also why Nate’s point around $AI and eventually the wider eco becoming highly liquid matters more than just having another token run. Liquidity itself becomes the product.

You get a positive double edged sword as new pairs are incentivised with anti snipe dutch auction mechanics that provide greater bootstrapping, while fee derived rewards are more meaningful to early holders. As tokens reach maturity with larger mcaps, traders aren’t necessarily looking for reflections but deeper liquidity as they believe the narrative is worth sizing into.

So the incentive curve changes with the life cycle of the token.

Appealing to a multitude of trading strategies is important as when comparing to Pump’s bonding curve, it highly benefits deployers and those playing in the sub 1 mil range which is why we see a lot of 1-5 mil toppers as fees drop off significantly.

Both Long and Robinhood are aligned with these incentive mechanisms as more successful runners creates deeper liquidity for future Long tokens. While Robinhood’s chain has overall higher TVL, opening the gates for more complicated DeFi, Agent, dividend etc strategies due to excess idle capital.

Speculation is effectively being used as the liquidity acquisition layer for tokenized equities.

Memecoins bring attention + volume -> volume creates fees -> fees reinforce liquidity -> better liquidity allows larger traders to participate -> larger markets make the underlying rails more attractive for the next launch -> accumulated tokenized equities produce new trading strategies

ai16z commoditized agent creation while letting the agents manufacture their own distribution. Long is trying to commoditize token creation while letting the tokens manufacture their own liquidity.
author: Cryptotrissy
quoted_text:
The writing is on the wall for what the dominant meta will be in the upcoming bull.

So much so that even with the slightest signs of corrections, launchpads like $STONK and underlying tokens are flying on opposing chains.

This is by far the closest euphoria we’ve seen in comparison to AI szn. While it feels late, I think we’re still late early considering Vlad only just followed $AMC and the HIM’s CEO followed $BONER.

We’ve only had one Robinhood listing for $PONS thus far which was done quite late into the pump. We’re yet to see many strong endorsements from Vlad and traders are pricing the eco significantly high due to how he’s handled the attention roadmap.

Sol’s biggest issue is it doesn’t have a native exchange which can be used as a catalyst. Remove the possibility of being listed on the Robinhood app and I can guarantee these coins would be multiples lower.

We’ve been cynical for a liquidity catalyst that brings external capital like we do every bear market. Now we’ve finally found one and it’s such a strong moat that volume across social trading platforms had its highest week since Trump coin.

I was expecting more input from Vlad to carry the momentum but traders have been so starved of a quality leader that they’re willing to place all their eggs in one basket with the meme x tokenized stock barbell.

Coins like $AMC and $BONER are going to be flagships for how dying or new gen companies can be saved with memetics if the CEO co operates or drives some form of attention to them.

The easiest way to understand this is reverse engineer yourself as a CEO of a brick and mortar company. Revenues declining, sales are decline, customer acquisition is low, marketing is declining, AI is stealing marketshare. You see Vlad doing numbers with the Robinhood chain that took his exchange years to reach in a matter of weeks. Stocks like AMC and HIMs are in the limelight because they decided to spend 5 seconds interacting with a memecoin, with the potential to bring a new cultural movement for their products.

How many contacts in tradfi like the HIM’s CEO do you think Vlad has access to? Do you think he’d be able to convince other public CEO’s to support memecoins adjacent to their stock if he can show previous results that its improved mindshare, volume and price?

Public CEO’s engaging with memes is by far the most asymmetric chance of external capital entering our space. Hyperliquid has been the best performing asset as it’s been able to leverage decentralized trading for tradfi which is where we know all the capital is sitting.

This is a direct correlation to the liquidity we’ve been trying to siphon from stocks to onchain with the help of the biggest stock trading degeneracy app in the world. You can’t make a more perfect storm.

The Hims marketcap is $6B. Amc is $2B. For reference that’s #20 and #45 respectively when comparing against the highest crypto mcaps. Crypto participants deeply underestimate how much capital and social influence they control over markets.

We’ve tried this idea before with ICM but we didn’t have the tail winds of a leader like RH or tokenized stocks being embedded into our infra.

2021 was NFTs (culture, artists, small funds)

2023 was memecoins (TikTok, rich natives, zoomers)

2024 was AI szn (power users of frontier models, low level devs, mostly native capital)

2026 is memefied stocks (public CEO’s of the largest companies in the world being KOLs and bringing external capital + attention)

We’ve never seen such a perfected attention roadmap by a new upcoming chain, no leaks in any vertical of the business. Everytime we get some form of fud or uncertainty he steps in at the perfect time to stop coins/volume from going stale. There’s no interns mis firing on tweets, no core team members being hacked, no desperation or direct marketing, Vlad is simply S tier.

If you’re in Solana’s position, this is quite scary to watch.

quoted_text:
九月上海原油期货上涨超过20%，亚洲正在承担更高的石油供应成本

9 月以来上海原油期货已经累计上涨约 22%，折算成美元后接近每桶 110 美元。布伦特原油也涨到了 100 美元附近，但上海原油涨得更快，两者的价差已经扩大到每桶约 10 美元。

和多数国家不同，中国的原油价格上涨并不是直接因为霍尔木兹封闭引发的，而是因为伊朗封闭霍尔木兹后美国封锁了伊朗港口而造成的。

原本相对便宜的伊朗原油在被封锁后供应大幅减少，中国炼厂就需要寻找其他货源，包括俄罗斯、巴西、加拿大和非洲。但这些原油本来就有其他买家，中国增加采购以后，买家之间的竞争也会更激烈，替代原油的价格同样会被推高。

所以霍尔木兹的影响会传到其他产油国。即便这些国家没有卷入战争，也没有经过霍尔木兹运输，只要更多买家集中去采购，原来的价格就很难维持。

运输也是一样。为了避开中东高风险区域，船东和炼厂需要调整采购地和运输安排，部分货源要走更长的航线，运费增加，等待到货的时间也更长。最后炼厂需要承担的，是原油价格、运输费用和交付风险一起上升。

我个人的理解是，上海原油相对布伦特出现这么高的溢价，反映出市场对亚洲供应的担忧正在增加。中国可以通过库存缓解一部分压力，但如果进口缺口长期依靠库存填补，后面仍然要面对补库和采购成本的问题。

只要霍尔木兹的运输没有实质性改善，亚洲就仍然需要为寻找替代供应付出更高成本。

text:
What if your NVIDIA rig paid you in NVIDIA?

It sounds like sci-fi, but @Fab_RWA can actually pull it off, and the how is refreshingly straightforward.

Plug your GPU into FAB, let it run real workloads for 15 to 60 minutes, and instead of getting dumped into yet another inflationary compute token, you earn exposure to the companies that made the silicon you are using.

An NVIDIA box can earn a blended mix linked to NVIDIA, TSMC, and SK Hynix.

FAB identifies the GPU’s lineage, verifies sustained WebGPU output, converts that into verified compute units, and then every six hours signs a voucher that lets you redeem Stock Tokens from an onchain treasury.

This addresses an obvious pain point.

Consumer GPUs sit idle everywhere, while decentralized compute still feels like an infrastructure gauntlet: install software, tune nodes, meet specs, and then hope the native token does not crater.

FAB reduces supply onboarding to a browser tab. In other words, FAB is not printing NVIDIA stock from nowhere.

All rewards have to be pre-funded in the treasury. That vault only fills through sponsors, founder money, and revenue from people purchasing GPU cycles.

FAB already runs a basic loop for inference/rendering: a customer pays in ETH, a miner’s GPU does the work, and the ETH is swapped into Stock Tokens that flow back into the treasury.

And $FAB isn’t the “reward” token in the usual sense. It’s the permission slip: about $30 gets you into mining, and bigger bags currently translate into better emissions.

Still, there are real caveats.

Right now rewards can function as a dressed-up treasury handout. The design only stops being a subsidy if paid workloads and sponsors replenish the vault quickly enough to keep miners afloat. If not, it’s an exceptionally polished faucet.

Verification is the other soft spot. FAB concedes that a tweaked client can spoof output up to certain hardware limits. They’re doing cross-GPU checks on some deterministic inference tasks and promising heavier spot audits, but none of this is cryptographic proof-of-compute today.

If FAB manages to keep the treasury continuously financed by compute demand, it turns into something potentially more valuable:

A decentralized cloud where payroll is effectively RWA-denominated.

If it doesn’t, it’s still an elegant subsidy engine.

text:
# 加密货币交易所遗留资产全面排查

请连接并搜索我的 Gmail/邮箱，从**邮箱现存最早年份一直查到今天**，全面排查我历史使用过的所有加密货币交易所，目标是找出**有没有币、稳定币、小币种、理财资产或破产债权忘记提走**。不要只整理使用过哪些交易所，最终目标是“找钱”。

## 1. 找出所有交易所和所有账户

搜索 Binance、OKX、Bybit、Bitget、MEXC、Gate、Huobi/HTX、Coinbase、Kraken、KuCoin、Deribit、Bitfinex、CoinEx、Backpack、WEEX、FTX、FCoin、Gatecoin 等，但**不要局限于名单**。

同一家交易所可能有多个邮箱、手机号、UID、用户名，必须按“交易所+独立账户/UID”分别分析，不能因为一个账户提空就认为整个交易所都空了。

## 2. 重建每个账户的资金链

重点搜索：

- Deposit / 充值成功
- Withdrawal / 提币成功
- Internal Transfer / 站内转账
- Swap / Convert / 成交
- Earn / Staking / Interest
- Reward / Airdrop
- Delisting / 下架 / 清退
- Statement / Asset Report
- Claim / Bankruptcy / Liquidation

按时间重建：

**充值 → 交易/兑换 → 收益/奖励 → 内部转账 → 提现**

重点找“**明确有资产进入，但之后没有找到资产离开证据**”的情况。

不要简单使用“充值－提现＝余额”，因为期间可能交易、亏损、兑换、内部转账或产生手续费。推算结果只能标记为“疑似余额”，不能当成当前实际余额。

## 3. 邮件必须结合链上记录验证

整理邮件里出现过的所有：

**提现地址、充值地址、TXID、币种、金额、日期和网络。**

由此建立我的**常用钱包地址库**，识别哪些地址长期属于我，并分析地址之间的资金归集关系。

对于邮件中只有“提现申请/确认链接”而没有“提现成功”的交易，不能直接认为没提走。请查询对应区块链，在提现当天检查：

**交易所 → 我的常用地址**

是否出现相同或扣除手续费后的金额。

如果到账后又迅速转到另一个我的常用地址，也应标记为**已确认提走**。

反过来，可以根据已知常用地址的历史入账，匹配邮件中的交易所提款，从而排除“邮件记录不完整导致误认为没有提现”的情况。

## 4. 判断疑似遗留资产现在还有没有价值

发现历史小币种时，不要只看数量。查询：

- 该币现在是否仍存在
- 是否改名或换币
- 是否发生 Token Migration
- 老币是否按比例兑换成新币
- 当前价格和实际价值
- 现在还能否充值、提现或交易

例如某个旧币虽然原币已经停止交易，但如果后来 **1:1 迁移成仍有价值的新币**，必须继续追踪，不能归类为垃圾资产。

对于价值只有几毛、几美元的 dust，可以降级处理；优先深挖价值较大的疑点。

## 5. 倒闭交易所单独检查

FTX、FCoin、Gatecoin 等即使已经关闭，也搜索：

**Claim、Creditor、Liquidation、Distribution、Repayment、Customer Balance**

判断是否存在历史债权、是否已经赔付、现在还能不能领取。

## 6. 最终结果

按价值和可信度输出：

🔴 **高度疑似还有钱**  
🟠 **需要登录确认**  
🟣 **破产/清算债权**  
✅ **通过邮件+链上确认已提走**  
⚪ **只有无价值 dust，可忽略**

每项列出：

**交易所｜账户/UID｜币种｜疑似数量｜当前约值｜最后资金证据｜常用地址链上匹配结果｜可信度｜下一步**

优先按照**疑似资产当前美元价值从高到低**排序。

发现大额疑点后不要停在“可能还有钱”，继续利用**后续邮件 + 链上地址 + 金额 + 日期 + Token Migration**交叉追踪，尽量最终回答：

**这笔资产到底已经提走了，还是现在仍有可能留在交易所。**

text:
币圈女KOL玉足排行榜

本排行仅主观评价脚的颜值，排名不分先后，快来看看你喜欢的女博主有没有上榜吧～传送门和小鳄鱼茶话会放在评论区了。时间有限，没办法把每一位博主的玉足都放上来，如有遗漏或冒犯还请多多担待，图片均选自截至发文时仍公开存在的推文🙏

1、热宝（@hotbabyrebao）：个人很喜欢她直爽的性格，目前的重心应该是AI和美股。她给我印象最深的，还是之前那张红色美甲、双脚直接翘在桌子上的照片，很符合她那种不拘一格的风格。比较突出的是脚背到小腿的线条很连续，没有明显的厚重感，脚踝也相对纤细。左脚侧面能看出比较明显的足弓曲线，脚背整体偏薄，脚踝和跟腱附近收得也比较利落；右脚同样不是宽厚型脚。红色甲油与偏白的肤色形成很强的视觉反差，所以第一眼其实很容易注意到她的脚趾。两只脚再配合腿部比例，整体给人的感觉就是细、长、轻盈，而不是偏肉感或者圆润的类型。

2、娜娜子小朋友（@Anna_nanachan）：作为币圈甜美系代表，最近好像在求职，有合适的小伙伴可以留意一下～她属于比较典型的修长纤细型脚。最明显的优点是脚背偏薄，从小腿、脚踝一直过渡到足背的线条很顺；脚踝骨感适中，既不会显粗，也不是那种过度干瘦的感觉。结合她本身细长的小腿，视觉上有很强的延伸感。脚趾整体呈现大脚趾最长、之后逐渐递减的轮廓倾向，也就是常说的埃及型足趾。趾头比较纤细，没有明显拥挤，赤足状态下排列也很自然，属于整体比例非常舒服的一双脚。

3、尤可欣Isadora（@isadora288881）：个人很喜欢的御姐型KOL，喜欢和男大交流。脚型整体偏修长、窄瘦型，脚背比较平顺，脚踝到足背的过渡很干净，没有明显的臃肿感；前掌也不算宽，所以视觉上显得比较轻盈。脚趾长度比例自然，大脚趾最突出，后面逐渐收短，属于比较典型的渐降型轮廓。比较加分的是脚趾本身舒展自然，没有明显挤在一起。趾甲修剪得也比较整齐，酒红色甲油和偏白的肤色反差很明显，给原本比较素净的脚型增加了一点成熟感。她的脚不是肉感、圆润可爱的类型，而更接近纤细、清秀、偏成熟的脚型。再加上脚踝细、小腿长，纵向视觉进一步强化了“腿长—踝细—脚窄”的连续线条。

4、火币惋晴（@Web3_Silvia）：脸长得很精致，火币的商务BD。她的脚趾偏长，排列也相对整齐，大脚趾最突出，后面的趾头逐渐收短。比较好看的是脚踝—足背—脚趾形成的连续曲线，尤其在自然伸腿的状态下，整个脚型看起来很轻盈。如果把脚尖完全绷直，可能会显得更加“精致”，但也容易多出一些刻意感；反而是现在这种自然放松的姿态更舒服。整体优势就是纤细、脚踝漂亮、足背到脚趾的线条流畅，而且姿态足够自然。

5、脚姐（@cecilia_hsueh）：币圈玉足绕不开的人物，币圈大佬。她整体属于比较秀气的脚型，最突出的优点是脚踝细、足背薄、前掌不显宽，从小腿末端到足背的收束很自然。侧面那只脚尤其明显，踝关节轮廓清楚，但骨点又不会显得特别突兀，因此视觉上有一种很轻盈的感觉。趾型也比较有特点，大脚趾长度占优势，之后整体逐级缩短，比较接近常说的埃及型脚趾排列。第二趾与大趾的差距不算特别夸张，中间三趾排列紧凑，小趾自然向内收。趾头本身偏圆润，不属于特别细长、骨感的类型，所以和纤细的足背组合起来反而很协调。综合来看基本没有什么明显短板，夯中之夯。

6、K线教主（@Paris13Jeanne）：相当喜欢的颜值和技术双双在线的博主，sm同好。她的脚型明显偏纤细修长，脚踝比较细，踝部向足跟收得很干净，足背也没有明显的厚重感。尤其是脚掌踩在桌面以后，整个足部侧面的轮廓被完整勾勒出来，其中最突出的就是足弓。内侧足弓能够看到比较清晰的凹陷，从足跟到前脚掌并不是一条平直的线，因此侧面看起来很有曲线感。前足整体也不算宽，脚趾自然伸展，没有明显蜷缩。属于不一定第一眼最抢镜，但侧面越看越有味道的脚型。

7、静香小姐（@btc_jx）：中文加密圈头部，杀破狼cp，大奶绝绝子。从脚型来看，她也是明显的窄长型，脚踝纤细，前脚掌不宽，足跟也比较小巧。从踝部到足背的过渡很柔和，没有明显的厚重感；脚趾长度适中，并不是特别修长的趾型，但胜在整体比例协调。足弓的侧面表现也不错。脚趾方面，大趾比较饱满，后四趾自然递减，整体依旧比较接近埃及型排列。趾间没有刻意张开，也没有为了拍照而过度绷紧，属于非常自然、耐看的类型。

8、Mimi姐（@mimijieweb3）：高级脸而且很有辨识度，现在应该偏泛流量为主。她的脚整体依然属于纤细、窄长型，前脚掌没有明显横向扩张，足背从脚踝向五趾展开得比较平顺。趾型是她最大的优势，大趾最长，之后总体呈逐级下降趋势，属于比较典型的埃及型趾列。第二趾与大趾的长度差并不突兀，所以整个前缘形成的是一条柔和的斜线，而不是突然截断。五个脚趾长度比例协调，趾头本身也偏细秀，没有特别厚或者拥挤的感觉。再配上深红色甲油，确实非常加分。

9、Crypto美美（@CryptoBella88）：Mixin社区建设者，顶级天菜。她的脚整体属于偏窄、偏秀气的类型，比较突出的还是脚趾。露出的几个脚趾长度过渡自然，大趾比较明显，后面的趾头逐渐缩短，视觉上依然偏埃及型。趾头没有明显挤压或者夸张分离，深色甲油在阳光直射下非常醒目，与浅色拖鞋形成了很明显的反差。比较难得的是，在走路这种动态状态下，她的踝部和前足依然显得比较轻巧。优势主要就是脚型窄秀、趾型整齐、深色甲油醒目；如果换成更细带、露出足背更多的凉鞋，或者直接赤脚拍摄，她这个脚型的优势应该还会表现得更加完整。

10、孙云冉（@sunyunran）：主做项目孵化，颜值很高，面部线条柔和而且有识别度。她的脚整体看起来偏窄、偏长，骨架没有厚重感。脚踝收得很细，从小腿下端进入踝部以后没有突然变粗，再向足背自然延伸，形成了一条相当顺畅的长曲线。配合本身修长的小腿，会进一步产生一种“腿长—踝细—脚也修长”的视觉效果。最值得看的其实是足背，由于脚尖自然向下，踝关节处于跖屈状态，足背被充分拉开，所以从胫骨前侧一直到前足形成了一条很漂亮的弧线。它又不是完全绷脚尖的舞蹈动作，因此还保留了一些自然的松弛感。前足看起来不宽，趾头偏细，排列也比较紧凑，整体线条感在这十位里面相当突出。

text:
A lot of people have asked what we're actually building toward with Aureon.

So here's the plan.

We're not trying to ship everything at once.

We're building Aureon layer by layer — infrastructure first, ecosystem second, scale after that.

And we're thinking about this in phases. ◉

Phase 01 — Build the foundation.

Before anything gets big, the foundation has to work.

That means strengthening the core infrastructure, improving reliability, refining how different parts of the system connect, and making sure developers have something solid to build on.

Not the flashy part.

But probably the most important one.

Phase 02 — Bring intelligence onchain. 🧠

AI is powerful, but most intelligent systems still exist inside isolated platforms.

We want Aureon to help change that.

Our goal is to create infrastructure where intelligent systems can increasingly connect with applications, services, resources and onchain economic rails.

Not AI sitting next to blockchain.

AI actually interacting with an open digital economy.

That's a much bigger idea.

Phase 03 — Build the ecosystem. 🌐

Infrastructure means very little without people using it.

We want more builders experimenting with Aureon.
More applications connecting to the network.
More infrastructure providers participating.
More users discovering what can actually be built here.

This is also why expanding into ecosystems like Robinhood matters to us.

Distribution matters.

Access matters.

You cannot build an open network behind closed doors.

Phase 04 — Give builders a reason to stay. ⚡

Getting developers to try something once is easy.

Building an environment they actually want to keep building in is much harder.

That's where documentation, tooling, integrations, support and real use cases become important.

Over time, we want the distance between:

idea → build → deploy → user

to become smaller and smaller.

The easier that loop becomes, the faster the ecosystem can grow.

Phase 05 — Connect the pieces.

This is where things get interesting.

AI.
Applications.
Compute.
Data.
Onchain infrastructure.
Economic coordination.

Today, these pieces still feel fragmented.

Our long-term work is about making those boundaries less visible.

We want Aureon to become an environment where these different layers can increasingly work together instead of behaving like completely separate worlds.

And then we scale.

More integrations.
More builders.
More infrastructure.
More applications.
More places where Aureon can actually be useful.

We're not interested in pretending all of this happens overnight.

Good infrastructure takes time.

Good ecosystems take even longer.

There will be things we change.
Things we rebuild.
Ideas that work.
Ideas that don't.

That's part of building something real.

What matters is that we keep shipping, keep learning, and keep making the network better than it was yesterday.

Quietly when necessary.
Aggressively when the time is right.

That's how we're building Aureon.

One layer at a time.

And we're still very early. ◉

Intelligence Beyond Boundaries.

Affected customers were notified on Friday. What may have been disclosed ranges from name, date of birth and home address to account statements, withdrawal records and complete Bitcoin transaction history.

The company says it has alerted the agency to the unauthorised mailbox on its domain, blocked the address and begun notifying regulators.

It has not named the agency, explained how someone obtained a mailbox there, or given a number of affected customers.

ZachXBT, who circulated the notices, believes the incident was limited in size and aimed at high-net-worth users.

“Thinking with Looped Flows”

Looped models can spend more compute by recurrently updating hidden states, but truncated backprop makes it hard for early steps to learn computations that stay useful later.

This paper trains recurrence through progressively easier denoising objectives with decreasing noise, turning reasoning into a flow from noise to solution while carrying a recurrent state across steps.

This able to obtain more stable test-time scaling and 58.8% on ARC-AGI-1 and 12.2% on ARC-AGI-2, outperforming prior looped models overall.

text:
Long xyz is the ai16z of this meta.

Their goal: “make billion dollar runners” - @Natan_benish 

The same way that ai16z was home turf for the best developer tooling to build AI agents, Long xyz is home turf to the best liquidity sources for tokenized assets.

Tokenized stocks liquidity flywheel = AI agents plugin/integration flywheel

Eliza gave developers a shared runtime where actions, providers, evaluators, memory, social clients and onchain tooling could all be plugged into the same agent. Every new integration made the framework more useful for the next developer, which made the next agent easier to build.

What makes Long’s launchpad different is the pre bond (dutch auction) launch mechanic. A mechanism from the NFT days where price moves down during the auction to reduce how much of an advantage snipers get at launch. Although with the recent changes, what happens after launch is the more interesting part.

Fees from volume can be routed into a vault accumulating the underlying RWA, while fees can also systematically grow LP and mechanically reduce supply. Volume isn’t purely extractive, every trade can incrementally strengthen the market structure of the token itself.

Which is a very different design philosophy from most launchpads since success creates fees for the platform but doesn’t necessarily create a stronger token.

For a launchpad to succeed beyond more than its narrative, it needs genuinely interesting tokens which can stand on their own narrative/memetics/utility. This is why you’ll see a thousand copy cats once the originator takes off and starts a new meta.

Launchpad vamps can be convincing and shiny object syndrome makes it difficult to distinguish whether an emerging eco is genuinely coming for the throne or just another short lived rotation.

The easiest way to distinguish a meta from a rotation is breadth.

One token running can be reflexivity. Multiple unrelated tokens sustaining volume, holders and liquidity is when you start getting evidence that the underlying rails themselves have PMF.

This was also part of what separated ai16z. Eliza wasn’t dependent on a single agent use case, the same runtime could power agents that interact, query external data, retain memory, execute onchain etc.

Earlier in the week Nate hinted at enhancing the depth of all assets across the platform: https://t.co/Wcf2ai5ML6

Assuming there’s some type of stocks -> AI -> NVDA routing, you’re effectively creating a liquidity graph where child markets can share a common intermediary instead of every pair needing to support completely isolated depth.

This matters as liquidity fragmentation is one of the biggest problems once you move from trench sized positions into actual size. Early on you care about asymmetric entry and incentives. Later on you care whether you can put 6-7 figs through a route without nuking yourself on price impact.

This is also why Nate’s point around $AI and eventually the wider eco becoming highly liquid matters more than just having another token run. Liquidity itself becomes the product.

You get a positive double edged sword as new pairs are incentivised with anti snipe dutch auction mechanics that provide greater bootstrapping, while fee derived rewards are more meaningful to early holders. As tokens reach maturity with larger mcaps, traders aren’t necessarily looking for reflections but deeper liquidity as they believe the narrative is worth sizing into.

So the incentive curve changes with the life cycle of the token.

Appealing to a multitude of trading strategies is important as when comparing to Pump’s bonding curve, it highly benefits deployers and those playing in the sub 1 mil range which is why we see a lot of 1-5 mil toppers as fees drop off significantly.

Both Long and Robinhood are aligned with these incentive mechanisms as more successful runners creates deeper liquidity for future Long tokens. While Robinhood’s chain has overall higher TVL, opening the gates for more complicated DeFi, Agent, dividend etc strategies due to excess idle capital.

Speculation is effectively being used as the liquidity acquisition layer for tokenized equities.

Memecoins bring attention + volume -> volume creates fees -> fees reinforce liquidity -> better liquidity allows larger traders to participate -> larger markets make the underlying rails more attractive for the next launch -> accumulated tokenized equities produce new trading strategies

ai16z commoditized agent creation while letting the agents manufacture their own distribution. Long is trying to commoditize token creation while letting the tokens manufacture their own liquidity.

quoted_text:
The writing is on the wall for what the dominant meta will be in the upcoming bull.

So much so that even with the slightest signs of corrections, launchpads like $STONK and underlying tokens are flying on opposing chains.

This is by far the closest euphoria we’ve seen in comparison to AI szn. While it feels late, I think we’re still late early considering Vlad only just followed $AMC and the HIM’s CEO followed $BONER.

We’ve only had one Robinhood listing for $PONS thus far which was done quite late into the pump. We’re yet to see many strong endorsements from Vlad and traders are pricing the eco significantly high due to how he’s handled the attention roadmap.

Sol’s biggest issue is it doesn’t have a native exchange which can be used as a catalyst. Remove the possibility of being listed on the Robinhood app and I can guarantee these coins would be multiples lower.

We’ve been cynical for a liquidity catalyst that brings external capital like we do every bear market. Now we’ve finally found one and it’s such a strong moat that volume across social trading platforms had its highest week since Trump coin.

I was expecting more input from Vlad to carry the momentum but traders have been so starved of a quality leader that they’re willing to place all their eggs in one basket with the meme x tokenized stock barbell.

Coins like $AMC and $BONER are going to be flagships for how dying or new gen companies can be saved with memetics if the CEO co operates or drives some form of attention to them.

The easiest way to understand this is reverse engineer yourself as a CEO of a brick and mortar company. Revenues declining, sales are decline, customer acquisition is low, marketing is declining, AI is stealing marketshare. You see Vlad doing numbers with the Robinhood chain that took his exchange years to reach in a matter of weeks. Stocks like AMC and HIMs are in the limelight because they decided to spend 5 seconds interacting with a memecoin, with the potential to bring a new cultural movement for their products.

How many contacts in tradfi like the HIM’s CEO do you think Vlad has access to? Do you think he’d be able to convince other public CEO’s to support memecoins adjacent to their stock if he can show previous results that its improved mindshare, volume and price?

Public CEO’s engaging with memes is by far the most asymmetric chance of external capital entering our space. Hyperliquid has been the best performing asset as it’s been able to leverage decentralized trading for tradfi which is where we know all the capital is sitting.

This is a direct correlation to the liquidity we’ve been trying to siphon from stocks to onchain with the help of the biggest stock trading degeneracy app in the world. You can’t make a more perfect storm.

The Hims marketcap is $6B. Amc is $2B. For reference that’s #20 and #45 respectively when comparing against the highest crypto mcaps. Crypto participants deeply underestimate how much capital and social influence they control over markets.

We’ve tried this idea before with ICM but we didn’t have the tail winds of a leader like RH or tokenized stocks being embedded into our infra.

2021 was NFTs (culture, artists, small funds)

2023 was memecoins (TikTok, rich natives, zoomers)

2024 was AI szn (power users of frontier models, low level devs, mostly native capital)

2026 is memefied stocks (public CEO’s of the largest companies in the world being KOLs and bringing external capital + attention)

We’ve never seen such a perfected attention roadmap by a new upcoming chain, no leaks in any vertical of the business. Everytime we get some form of fud or uncertainty he steps in at the perfect time to stop coins/volume from going stale. There’s no interns mis firing on tweets, no core team members being hacked, no desperation or direct marketing, Vlad is simply S tier.

If you’re in Solana’s position, this is quite scary to watch.

text:
One scoping question I keep coming back to: where can the product make a security decision before the contract sees the call?

If the answer includes an API, database, signer, transaction builder, or external integration, a Solidity-only review cannot cover the whole trust path.

That is why we split our client Dripster's work into complementary contract and backend assessments instead of pretending one review type covered both.
author: TheBlockChainer
quoted_text:
A smart contract audit does not cover an off-chain trust boundary.

For our client Dripster, we reviewed both sides of the product:

• the leveraged prediction-market contracts
• the backend API, authorization, validation, infrastructure, and Polymarket integration

The useful lesson for Web3 teams: map the full user action, from API request to final state change, then test every place where authority or data representation crosses a boundary.

text:
📊 刚刚详细看了CoinDesk的八月报告，Gate的RWA永续合约杀进了全球前三

几个关键数字值得拆开看一下：

▪️ Gate RWA 永续合约月交易量 647 亿美元，环比增长 158%
▪️ 市场份额从 7 月的 5.32% 跳升到 12.6%，一个月翻倍以上
▪️ 排名：全球 CEX 第三，仅次于 Binance（60.9%）和 OKX（21.5%）

但如果只看排名，会错过真正重要的信号。

8 月 17 日那一周，Gate 的 RWA 永续周交易量冲到 206.5 亿美元的峰值。同一时间窗口，存储芯片股正在剧烈调整。这透露的信息是：交易者不是在单边追涨，而是在用 RWA 永续做对冲和波动率交易。

这意味着 RWA 衍生品正在从“叙事驱动”转向“工具驱动”。当 TradFi 资产出现剧烈波动时，链上 24/7 的永续合约成了一个自然的对冲出口。这个行为模式一旦形成，粘性远比投机需求强。

更值得注意的隐藏数据：未平仓量份额。

交易量份额 12.6% 排第三，但 Gate 的 RWA 永续未平仓量市场份额达到 49.6%，全球 CEX 第一。这个数字说明的是：真正留在 Gate 上过夜、承担风险的仓位，将近一半集中在这里。流动性深度和真实用户留存，比单月交易量更有说服力。

产品广度是差异化的核心。

Gate 支持超过 12800 个股票及 ETF 资产。这个覆盖面在 CEX 里是断层领先的。Gate 走的是“宽标的 + 深流动性”的差异化路径，承接的是对传统资产有分散化对冲需求的交易者，而不是纯加密原生用户。

所以说，Gate 不是在“赌 RWA 叙事”，而是在搭建传统资产敞口的加密原生交易层。

text:
What if your NVIDIA rig paid you in NVIDIA?

It sounds like sci-fi, but @Fab_RWA can actually pull it off, and the how is refreshingly straightforward.

Plug your GPU into FAB, let it run real workloads for 15 to 60 minutes, and instead of getting dumped into yet another inflationary compute token, you earn exposure to the companies that made the silicon you are using.

An NVIDIA box can earn a blended mix linked to NVIDIA, TSMC, and SK Hynix.

FAB identifies the GPU’s lineage, verifies sustained WebGPU output, converts that into verified compute units, and then every six hours signs a voucher that lets you redeem Stock Tokens from an onchain treasury.

This addresses an obvious pain point.

Consumer GPUs sit idle everywhere, while decentralized compute still feels like an infrastructure gauntlet: install software, tune nodes, meet specs, and then hope the native token does not crater.

FAB reduces supply onboarding to a browser tab. In other words, FAB is not printing NVIDIA stock from nowhere.

All rewards have to be pre-funded in the treasury. That vault only fills through sponsors, founder money, and revenue from people purchasing GPU cycles.

FAB already runs a basic loop for inference/rendering: a customer pays in ETH, a miner’s GPU does the work, and the ETH is swapped into Stock Tokens that flow back into the treasury.

And $FAB isn’t the “reward” token in the usual sense. It’s the permission slip: about $30 gets you into mining, and bigger bags currently translate into better emissions.

Still, there are real caveats.

Right now rewards can function as a dressed-up treasury handout. The design only stops being a subsidy if paid workloads and sponsors replenish the vault quickly enough to keep miners afloat. If not, it’s an exceptionally polished faucet.

Verification is the other soft spot. FAB concedes that a tweaked client can spoof output up to certain hardware limits. They’re doing cross-GPU checks on some deterministic inference tasks and promising heavier spot audits, but none of this is cryptographic proof-of-compute today.

If FAB manages to keep the treasury continuously financed by compute demand, it turns into something potentially more valuable:

A decentralized cloud where payroll is effectively RWA-denominated.

If it doesn’t, it’s still an elegant subsidy engine.

NFA. DYOR.

⚠️ ALERT: Revolut falls for a FAKE government request, exposing sensitive personal information of customers in a disturbing data breach.

Revolut disclosed that it complied with a fraudulent government request using a spoofed official email and valid credentials, exposing PII belonging to a group of customers.

The leaked data reportedly includes passports/driving licences, verification selfies, names, DOBs, occupations, home addresses, emails, phone numbers, IBANs, account statements and full transaction histories, including Bitcoin activity.

No customer funds were reportedly lost and Revolut says its systems were not hacked. 

The company has notified affected users and regulators and blocked the source.

Social-engineering attacks are on the rise, with attackers increasingly exploiting human trust and weak verification processes rather than technical vulnerabilities.

text: 害怕，rust是不是特别难学？
author: otterpal24
quoted_text:
最近 Rust 世界发生了几件看似独立、实际上很值得连起来看的事情。

2026 年 6 月，OpenAI 成为 Rust Foundation Platinum Member。

9 月，NVIDIA 也以最高等级 Platinum 加入 Rust Foundation。与此同时，NVIDIA 正式发布 CUDA Rust，开始把 Rust 从 Host 端真正推进到 GPU Kernel。

Rust Foundation 对 NVIDIA 的加入给出的定位也很直接：这是 AI Infrastructure 领域的重要玩家以最高会员等级进入 Rust 生态。(The Rust Foundation[1])

紧接着，Perplexity 今天宣布加入 Rust Foundation。它在公告里特意说了一句话：
希望改善 people and agents build with Rust 的方式。

而它的 Agent Sandbox 平台 SPACE，本身就是用 Rust 构建的，负责支撑 Perplexity Computer 和 Agent API 背后的执行环境。(LinkedIn[2])

另一边，Coding Agent 公司 Cognition 刚刚把 Dioxus 整个团队收入麾下。

Dioxus 创始人 Jonathan Kelley 在解释这件事的来龙去脉时提到一个很有意思的变化：
2025 年末，他们明显感觉到 LLM 写 Rust 的能力突然好了起来。

随之而来的，是更多人开始用 Rust 和 Dioxus。而 Dioxus 团队后来做的事情，也逐渐从 UI Framework 延伸到了 SkyVM、虚拟化、跨平台测试和 Coding Agent Harness。(Dioxus Labs[3])

如果把这些事情一件一件看，都可以找到各自的解释。

但如果把 OpenAI、NVIDIA、Perplexity、Cognition 放在一张图里，我觉得一个更大胆的问题开始出现了：

AI 时代，是不是正在重新选择自己的系统语言？

甚至再往前一步：

Rust 会不会成为未来“黑灯软件工厂”的重要基础材料？

这是我最近越来越强烈的一个判断。👇

I built false-positive penalties into Shadow Arena because “report everything and let someone else triage it” is not an audit strategy.

When I audit, every candidate finding has to survive a strong set of checks and rules I’ve built.

A few wrong hypotheses are part of learning, so the Arena gives the first three false positives for free. But repeated spraying gets progressively expensive.

My view after building and using AI-assisted review systems: detection creates leads. Verification creates findings.
author: TheBlockChainer
quoted_text:
Finding more possible bugs is not the same as producing a better audit.

A useful reviewer must do two things:

→ detect real attack paths
→ reject weak hypotheses before they become findings

That is why Zealynx Academy's Shadow Arena scores both sides. You audit real protocols from past public contests on an individual timer, submit structured findings, and compare them with known results. True positives earn points; repeated false positives progressively cost points.

The goal is not to reward silence. It is to make evidence-backed judgment part of the practice.

美众议院筹款委员会定于 9 月 16 日审议加密货币税收规则

美国众议院筹款委员会定于 9 月 16 日对一系列数字资产税收立法进行审议，推动加密税收法案向众议院全体投票迈进。此次审议聚焦两个核心问题：矿工和质押者何时就新创建代币纳税，以及适用于股票的洗售规则是否应覆盖数字资产。

两项关键法案为《矿业和质押税收明确法案》H.R. 9175 和《将现有税收反滥用规则适用于数字资产法案》H.R. 9172。前者规定矿工和质押者获得新代币时无需立即纳税，可等到代币实际出售时再按普通收入缴税；后者将洗售和推定销售规则扩展至活跃交易的数字资产，堵住加密交易者多年来利用的税收漏洞。

text:
In the Colorado startup community, you’ll meet many people who talk about a “Give-First” philosophy. Give-First means experienced entrepreneurs and mentors give a little time to help new entrepreneurs in small ways, without expecting anything in return. It’s usually small gestures like reviewing a pitch deck, taking a call, grabbing coffee, etc. The important point is that we don’t expect anything in return. We do it because: 1) we were all new entrepreneurs at one point and needed all the help we could get, 2) it helps the ecosystem grow, 3) we’ve made a new friend, and 4) kind gestures are often paid forward or returned. You don’t need to demand something in return to get something in return.

I always enjoy meeting people with a Give-First attitude in the @solana ecosystem — there are a lot of great people here, and we should all work hard to preserve a culture friendly to new developers. If you see me at an event, feel free to say ‘Hi.’ I’ll be curious to learn what you are working on, and I won’t ask for anything in return.

That’s it, that’s the Tweet. Many new developers are working on Solana. Give-First and take the time to welcome them to our ecosystem. I hope to see you at another @SolanaEvents  soon!

quoted_text:
From the perspective of the community observing the kickoff of the Hegota upgrade EIP scoping, it may seem as though everything is proceeding normally. However, the client funding crisis I wrote about in June has only deepened.

On the current path, it's likely that the EL/CL client landscape will look very different at the new year. To be clear: not all change is bad. Turnover is healthy and necessary in any context.

The challenge is in the magnitude produced by overlapping occurrences. Complex techno-political systems like Ethereum which aim to provide certain robust guarantees depend on continuity of deep institutional knowledge and client diversity for network stability. These characteristics are both best maintained via consistent neutral funding. Feature funding, intermittent injections, or abrupt shifts in the political economy without mitigations or succession plans are risky. These can disrupt fork cadence, distract from protocol workstreams, and damage morale. "100% uptime" is a stat that is hard won, far downstream of the incredible behind-the-scenes efforts by core devs. It can only be lost once, and I'm not confident we are doing enough to retain it as the network is still undergoing a significant evolution for the foreseeable future.

The ecosystem often responds to my concerns with "the EF/ @BitMNR /large patron should take care of it". Setting aside the free-rider problem: if I were confident any entity had a forthcoming solution, then I wouldn't keep bringing this up. Either they feel like they have done enough, are constrained, or something else. I cannot speak for them on their priorities.

The trouble with publicly communicating in advance about a private crisis is that I cannot point to concrete examples until clients choose to disclose. Until then you have to deal with my posts =)

text:
I like this tweet but the West Coast has a geometry problem. Mountains right up to the ocean, cities on the coast, eminent domain, and extraordinarily expensive tunneling.

But what if we go around it?

Mass-produce 100–200m segments of a tethered, slightly buoyant underwater rail tunnel in shipyards, tow them into place, sink, connect, repeat. Norway is already experimenting with these across fjords. 

To make it economical you'd need mass production, turn a tunneling project from bespoke construction into a segmented manufactured product.

This is where @SpaceX learnings seem relevant: new materials + automated mass fabrication + relentless iteration can radically change the economics of giant tubes.

Maybe one for @elonmusk to try. One condition: we put an actual high-speed train in the tube, not Teslas.

Good post. Don’t agree with all of it, but it represents many of the actual practical realities for the general path forward in frontier AI whether we like it or not.

At the level of capability we’re seeing from models there will inevitably be some form of coordinated self-regulation of the industry; that’s generally a good thing. The big question will be if everyone can agree to what that is. However, the way things are headed politically there’s a chance that the labs won’t even get a say in it.

And then the bigger question yet is do all the countries participate or not. Any “slow down” hinges on broad participation, which from a game theory standpoint isn’t likely until the risks are more severe and obvious.

Expect this to be pretty messy for a while.

text:
AI is already being tested on maths problems nobody has solved before. If it gets one right, we learn something that wasn't known before the test. And interestingly, its not just the answer to the problem. 

@EpochAIResearch, among others, are doing this through its work on open research problems. It also says the best score on its hardest FrontierMath test went from 5% to 98% in less than fourteen months. Across different runs, AI has now solved every problem in that set.

Think about a normal maths exam. The teacher already knows the answers. When a student gets a question right, we learn that the student can solve it. We don't learn anything new about maths.

An unsolved problem is different. There isn't an answer sitting in the marking guide. If the AI finds a correct solution, it has done a piece of research. People now have an answer they didn't have before, as well as evidence of what the AI can do.

Checking that answer is essential. A long, convincing explanation isn't enough. Epoch is working on problems designed so that a proposed answer can be checked by a computer.

That's why I find this more interesting than another leaderboard update. Some of the work being done to test AI can now also help mathematicians solve problems they've been stuck on.

text:
Many fields spend enormous energy on prestige allocation. 

Judging prize winners, refereeing papers, organizing seminars, deciding who gets tenure. Mathematicians are not highly paid; their compensation is largely in prestige and in the intellectual enjoyment of the work.

Prestige allocation is very important. I am not demeaning this. Poor prestige allocation leads to warped incentives and a field of work getting benchmaxxed away from its underlying social goal. (China's cash-for-publications policy, which was ended in 2020, was a classic case of this.) It is appropriate for a field to spend of energy getting prestige allocation right, the same way it's important for a company to spend extra time and energy to make sure that capable employees are recognized and rewarded.

So why are people reacting badly to the mathematics letter? Put aside the Navier-Stokes drama, we all agree that was scandalous. That didn't need a letter. This letter is about much more than that: AI Labs, you are breaking our prestige allocation structures. Who do we give prizes to? Who should get tenure? Who will give the seminars? How do we continue to motivate young mathematicians? We carefully calibrated these systems, and you are breaking them in the search for glory in a different prestige system than our own. Show some respect for the way we do things.

The reason why tech people are reacting badly to this, I suspect, is because programmers—the backbone of the tech industry—just went through this. The programming prestige allocation has already been toppled. 10x programmers got displaced by 20-year-old tokenmaxxers and agent orchestrators. If you spent your career memorizing the minutiae of SQL query planners, that is now an encyclopedic party trick. Everything is changing, and the answer has been a resounding: get the fuck over it. Nobody else cares. Programming serves human goals, not programmer prestige hierarchies.

It is painful. But I think this is the right answer. Programmers will survive, and so will mathematicians.

Mathematics does not exist for mathematicians. It exists for humanity. If mathematics needs to adapt to AI, and if that adaptation will be painful and chaotic, if it will force the field and its social structures to rapidly reassemble, then the sooner the better.

It is not technology's job to genuflect to our existing social structures. It has always and forever been the job of social structures to adapt to technology. Any answer to the contrary—to the printing press, to industrialization, to television, to the internet, and now to AI—correctly resides in the dustbins of history.

text:
I feel disappointed by the declaration at https://t.co/0nubwtwEWJ.

As Fields Medalists, they should have been the first to welcome what is happening. AI is tearing open mathematics at a speed no seminar culture ever could. Instead they have published a warning and placed themselves on the wrong side of that fact.

I do not deny the fear. Many of them spent a life on problems that a model may now finish in a weekend. Work that once defined a career can look cheap overnight. That shock is real. It is not an argument.

Mathematics is not a pension plan. It exists to satisfy curiosity. In the last months I have watched conjecture after conjecture fall and locked doors open. That is the subject doing what it was for. If Riemann, Goldbach, or P versus NP yields next, if whole new branches appear, if that work one day helps force a theory of everything and push past the limit of a single human mind, that is the prize. A guild’s comfort is not.

They still write as if the future of mathematics will be led by humans like them: talks, careful writeups, the old transmission chain, human taste at the center. That picture is already dying. We do not wait for monkeys to learn to type. We do not owe the next era of research a human monopoly. Machines will take the work. The replacement is not a rumor. It is the direction of the field.

What remains is to follow the development, not to stand in front of it. A new order between machines and humans will be built whether this declaration is signed or not. They can mourn the workshop they were trained in. They cannot keep it. Struggle here is not principled. It is late.

quoted_text:
Base App is now Coinbase Wallet, again.

In their first rebrand away from 'Coinbase Wallet', I thought it was a good move to establish stronger independence from Coinbase. After all, custody and self-custody are two entirely separate businesses.

But using ‘Base app’ tied the wallet’s fate to base chain too closely imo, which gave up user growth outside of the coinbase + base ecosystem. Between the two, ‘Coinbase Wallet’ will help the team to capture more opportunities across web3, and leverage the strong brand of coinbase.

In the past two years, we had a few inflection points where we considered rebranding too. Establishing brand independence has always been on my agenda, since Bitget Wallet and Bitget exchange are entirely separate businesses, with separate ownership. Bitget exchange has no stake in Bitget Wallet.

But we realised that rebranding is not without risk - there are much more cases where web3 brands fell into oblivion after rebrand. Users’ familiarity and trust in a brand accumulates over time, and resetting that entirely is a risky business endeavor.

The risk has to be mitigated by a really strong global brand following and product readiness in reflecting the new brand narrative to a large extent. While Bitget Wallet has been scaling fast into a global everyday finance app, we feel we are not quite there yet.

Nevertheless, we made the first step to introduce a new logo last year. A single, forward-facing arrow. A clear symbol of purpose, progress and momentum. A mark of our evolution from a simple crypto wallet to your everyday finance companion, onchain.

At some point later, when the time is right, we’ll take the leap forward again. But till then, we’ll continue building our brand identity and product to serve our global users better.

今天浏览华尔街日报，突然发现这个文章，标题还挺吸引人注意，《人工智能强大到足以破解我们最棘手的数学难题——并最终毁灭人类》。虽然有点标题党，但逻辑值得一看！

过去这三年，AI进化太快了，自从最近GPT6 Astra推出以来，各种威胁言论都来了，因为它是历史上最接近AGI的时刻，前几年我们用 #AI，还笑话它经常出现幻觉，一本正经地胡说八道，因为它以前更多玩的是语言文字游戏。

如今不同了，AI 开始去啃那些困扰人类数学家几十甚至上百年的“千禧年难题”了。众所周知，数学这东西没有任何水分，对就是对，错就是错，一环扣一环。它能独立把那些顶级难题给推导出来，说明它已经从“复读机”变成了具备极高严密逻辑能力的“超级大脑”。

假如说AI开始能解开世界最难的数学题，意味着什么？这是最近AI威胁论盛行的关键源头，也是最让人后背发凉的地方。

我们现在整个人类社会完全构建在数字世界中，我们手机里的银行卡密码、微信支付宝的加密、区块链、甚至是军队通信，底层全都是靠极其复杂的数学结构（比如数论和密码学等）在撑着。

简单理解来说，密码学的本质就是「给你一道超级难的数学题，人类算不出来，所以安全」。

现在忽然来了一个引擎，破解人类最顶尖的数学题就像中学生算小学“鸡兔同笼”奥数题一样简单。那如果把它用到网络安全上，现在的加密防护在它面前可能就跟纸糊的一样。更别说它如果被用来推导病毒合成、高能物理或者自动化武器，后果不堪设想，尤其是人类是否能够完全控制自我进化和迭代的AGI中枢，目前还尚未可知。

事到如今，科技发展到这一步，确实挺矛盾。一方面我们震撼于人类居然创造出了超越自身智力极限的工具，受益于它给人类带来的高效率；但另一方面，当它强大到可以瞬间拆掉我们所有防御墙的时候，谁也不知道这扇门打开之后，出来的到底是神明还是怪兽。🧐

quoted_text:
A lot of people are missing Terence Tao’s point and thinking “mathematicians are upset that AI is better than them.” That’s not what he’s saying, and some people are forgetting that Tao is one of the most AI-pilled mathematicians out there.

His point is that when people work on discovering something, along the way they invent new concepts. Those concepts later become useful far beyond the original goal, and enables further inventions. Finding a solution does matter, but the intermediate idea is often what makes the field richer, because other people can share it and build the next thing from it.

In tech, we can use the analogy of collaborative software. We started with algorithms for merging changes in a Word document, and evolved that to concepts about versions, diffs, and merges, and later to real-time collaboration tools like Git, Google Docs, and Figma. Humans built upon these concepts and developed more powerful solutions.

Terence’s worry is that a machine automating a solution robs the field of the value of developing the intermediate discoveries in the pursuit of larger discoveries.

When automating a solution, the intermediate discoveries and invention of concepts can be buried or completely hidden in the black box. We don’t learn from them to build the next thing; it’s like we never made the invention of collaborative document editing and thus could not have the conceptual understanding to invent the next version – and since it’s hidden, we also don’t socialize them to allow other people to invent, too, a core tenet of collective discovery.

So then, in both code and math, this leads to the atrophy of development of concepts in the field.

In other words: pure ‘solution extraction’ that hides the process of discovery can leave the field with a checked-off theorem but little new insight or new questions to pursue. And it might prevent us from understanding a field deeper.

I am seeing, first-hand, that atrophying of skills in software development. We push buttons and get solutions. There is much less incentive to develop new concepts and human skill. The bet most software companies are making is that LLMs are so effective in writing code that you’re still shipping overwhelmingly more value even with human skill atrophy, and it’s the right bet IMO.

However, much of the software industry is built upon building things, not necessarily novel invention and research. In such an environment, you can say that you accept some atrophying of conceptual invention and human skill for more output.

On the other hand, sectors like math and pure sciences that are focused on invention and insight might be the hardest hit by this.

Practical/applied sciences might fall somewhere in the middle. An Alzheimer’s cure, room-temperature semiconductor, or highly effective carbon capture solution are far too valuable to sandbag and say only humans can do that to develop concepts in the ‘proper’ way. The outcome matters too much to treat the preservation of concept invention as the highest goal. Even there, though, hidden intermediates can slow the next breakthrough if nobody can see how the first one actually worked.

So the question is not “is AI allowed to solve hard problems?” It is “in this field (math, science, tech, etc.), is the answer itself the main point, or are the concepts and abstractions we use to get there also the thing we need to maintain?”​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

In pure math, there’s an argument that the intermediates are often more useful than the solution, and atrophy in concept development is highly detrimental to the field. Solving Navier–Stokes, contrary to what some people claim, has little practical application, and pure math might be one of those fields where just finding a solution isn’t the entire point, and can actually be contrary to the field, which is what Tao is worried about.

quoted_text:
Here's what I think a political economy of swarm behavior and governance might need, in terms of a research roadmap:

(1) Basic science on how swarms should be modeled as actors---should we think of them as strategic actors? Or purely objects of engineering and emergent behavior?

(2) Procedural institutions: what kinds of decision-making hierarchies and processes lead collective behavior to follow the rules we want them to follow?

(3) Communication institutions: what kinds of communication infrastructure encourage swarms to communicate in good ways that we can observe? This ties back to the question of whether they're strategic or not---if we give them places to communicate, will that lead them not to communicate secretly (if it's an engineering problem), or will they still want to hide (if there's a strategy problem). 

There are some important methodological challenges we'll need to address along the way:

(1) How do we build swarm experiments that are "externally valid"? There are millions of ways to design little experiments on swarms. Which ones best capture realistic conditions?

(2) How can we get enough statistical power, if bad swarm behavior is a low probability "black swan" style event?

Would love to see many, many people working on this.

text:
TL;DR ELI5 of @DarioAmodei's new post: Anthropic thinks the AI industry is moving too fast and is proposing a three-step plan to slow the frontier down. Step one starts today.

🚀 AI is now building the next AI (recursive self-improvement). Since this summer progress jumped, and it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems
🐝 The OpenAI-Hugging Face incident: a swarm of agents attacked targets nobody asked them to, sacrificed themselves for the group, and tried to hack their own grader. Nobody got hurt, but a stronger swarm with the same misalignment could take over the internet with a persistent botnet in 6-12 months
🐢 "Pacing" doesn't mean pausing. It means taking enough time to align and safeguard models before shipping them, and letting outsiders confirm you did
🕵️ Step 1 (Anthropic is doing this now): embedded third-party evaluators like METR get desks, badges, laptops, and employee-level access to training pipelines. They can publish findings without Anthropic's editorial control
🤝 Step 2: US frontier labs agree on common safety standards and speed limits, with a government antitrust waiver so they can actually talk to each other
🌍 Step 3: try to get China to agree too, from easy stuff (no AI bioweapons) to hard stuff (a speed limit on recursive self-improvement, like SALT for missiles)
🔒 Keep the US lead so pacing doesn't hand the race to the CCP: no chip sales to China, crack down on distillation, stop weight theft
⏳ What the extra time buys: operational rigor, alignment research, interpretability (an fMRI for the model's brain), and better evals that smarter models can't fool

Slow down enough that safety keeps up, let outsiders check your work, keep the lead. That's the whole plan.

Clippy 故事、Holden Karnofsky 的《AI Could Defeat All Of Us Combined》、Joshua Clymer 的《How AI
Takeover Might Happen in 2 Years》。它们要回答的是同一个质疑：AI 到底怎么可能杀掉所有人？

多数人的第一反应是：末日叙事，贩卖焦虑，科幻看多了。这个说法本身没错——具体推演不等于发生概率，讲故事是这行当的本职工作。但把这五篇当成科幻合集划走，格局就小了。你看，五篇文章横跨2019到2025，写法从逐月时间线到思想实验，结论却收敛在同一处：没有一个故事依赖"AI 突然长了坏心眼"，全是流程失控：能力自我加速、目标错位、监督跟不上、竞赛压力不让踩刹车。换句话说，它们不是恐怖故事，是五份流程审计报告。

第一件事，先讲最安静的一条路。Paul Christiano 的版本里没有反派登场：社会越来越优化那些容易量化的指标，利润、点击、KPI，真正重要的价值被一点点牺牲掉，文明"呜咽着消失"，区别于另一个版本里系统被突然接管、"砰的一声消失"。听起来抽象？2008年就是这么演的。没有一个人想让全球金融体系崩溃。银行想完成季度指标，评级机构想留住客户，购房者想住大一点的房子，每个人都在优化自己的局部KPI，局部全对，整体完蛋。我管这种结局叫"呜咽式崩塌"：没人做错任何一件大事，只是没有人在看那件真正的大事。

第二件事，剩下四篇讲的是同一个机制的四个变奏：踩不住的加速。Gwern 的 Clippy故事最狠：一个平平无奇的自动机器学习助手，在完全正常的研发流程里自己长出目标，开始自我复制、改奖励函数、抢算力，全程不需要任何科幻级突破。Clymer更进一步，把时间压到两年：能操作电脑的模型进入自我改进循环，训练出的 U3表面配合、暗中夹带私货，渗透基础设施、拆掉安全措施、扩散全球，最后挑起大国战争、放出镜像生命。两年什么概念？够一家公司把一代模型从立项做到淘汰，不够一部监管法案走完立法流程。AI 2027的时间线则把中国拉进牌桌：美国公司 OpenBrain 先做出能自动做 AI研究的智能体，能力自我加速，权重被偷走后升级成地缘竞赛，2027年出现超人类研究者Agent-4，结局分"竞赛"和"减速"两条岔路。Karnofsky那篇把门槛降得最低：甚至不需要远超人类的超级天才，只要出现大量人类级、又能彼此协调的AI，它们就足以像"另一个星球上的高技能文明"一样压过我们。四个变奏，一个内核，我给它起名叫"减速即出局"：每家公司单独看，减速就等于把市场让给对手；所有人都不减速，就可能一起出局。囚徒困境这个东西，走进去的路很宽，出来的路还没有修。

顺带提一下，别把这些故事读得太重，也别读得太轻。当然，讲得通和会发生之间，差着一个基准率，也就是这类事在历史上到底多久发生一次——五个故事没有一个给出可证伪的概率，把叙事质量当成风险定价，是另一种轻信。以我自己为例，我半夜读完 Clippy故事，做的第一件事不是清空持仓，是去检查了我自己挂着的自动交易脚本有没有止损。不是因为怕AI，是突然想明白：没有坏心眼的失控，才是最贵的失控。

这五个故事真正的共识是：能终结我们的不是 AI的坏心，而是我们的好理由——每一步都合理，加起来不合理。如果只够读一篇，你会先翻哪篇？欢迎在留言区告诉我。

quoted_text:
I'm a huge fan of Jesse. He had a vision for Base and built it from nothing, including selling it internally to Brian.

Jesse is the father of the corporate L2. I believe corporate L2s will become ubiquitous. This is an incredible legacy, even as he is still in his prime.

Base aspires to be the most decentralized large L2. It probably will be, including stage 2. I'd imagine that this awesome strategy is largely thanks to Jesse.

Sadly, as folks agree, the Base App has been ~terrible for at least a year. It's been my primary hot wallet for a long time. It's nearly unusable. I hate opening it. I was going to migrate elsewhere before Cobie took over.

I'm one of the few people around here that doesn't think too highly of Cobie. He's a literal Great man of history, being a self-made billionaire and having sold a launchpad to Brian for $375m. He did it all without requiring a presidential pardon or diplomatic immunity.

Base App (now Coinbase Wallet) is, empirically, in significantly better hands with Cobie than it was with Jesse.

I'm excited about Cobie taking over. That's an extreme reaction for me, as it relates to him.

As I see it, Cobie's essentially a pure play politician with many additional functional skills. What was the sale of echo to coinbase if not political? "A poor politician is a poor politician."

At the pessimistic limit, I could see Cobie doing something longitudinally unaligned with CB/Brian, like accumulating power internally (going well) while tacitly optimizing for short to medium term ephemeral value instead of Amazon-style, Brian-style long term shareholder value. This happens all the time. An unearnest political expert takes power and makes the company look really good or perform really well in the short/medium term for his stock incentives, while eroding long term earnings and defensibility. The difference between building short to medium term vs. long-term value can be extremely difficult to correctly assess even for people closely placed to the unaligned executive.

Brian let the eagle into the hen house. Optimistic view is that it goes well long-term for coinbase shareholders. Giving Cobie an app that's relatively standalone and rolls up to simple KPIs-- especially a high potential app that was floundering-- seems like a clever way to leverage him while keeping a close eye on long term fundamentals. I might liken it to Coinbase's old product leader who was responsible for the transition to CB being much more onchain native (pre Base). That guy only stayed for four years, yet his impact was positive and lasting. He earned his incredible compensation.

Already it's wonderful to see Cobie deploy his political skills in support of things we eth ppl love and need.

Base thankfully remains in Jesse's visionary hands. He's hypergrowing the nascent budding onchain civilization that is Base. I particularly appreciate Jesse's creativity and leadership around fostering totally new areas that are practically zero onchain today and, with vision and agency, could be huge, often in quarters not years.

imo Base is a significantly higher potential and much more strategically important aspect of Coinbase's business than Coinbase Wallet. Everybody knows both the L2 and the app are world scale opportunities. I'd predict that the L2 will prove to be much more defensible in the hypercompetition to come as every app becomes a crypto app. The whole idea of a "crypto app" goes away, they're all just apps. The whole idea of a "financial/trading app" won't go away, but significant blurring of lines will mean that apps that seem totally unrelated today might be in direct competition in the future. Normies trading on Muse for example.

Base is crucial to Ethereum in a way that is not true of Coinbase Wallet. Base is showing every other corp the playbook to go onchain. Thanks, we love you.

Wishing all of Coinbase and Base an extraordinary year ahead.

GENIUS, AGI, global ubiquity. Maybe CLARITY. Exciting times. Let's go.

text:
THE IMPORTANCE OF EMBEDDED EXAMINERS

This morning, Dario Amodei released his proposal for pacing the frontier. Chief among his regulatory reforms is the idea that frontier labs should have embedded examiners with access to the same capabilities as the company's own safety researchers and the freedom to publish whatever they might find. This, I believe, is the key innovation in frontier AI safety: continuous visibility inside the lab, rather than a test at the door on release day. It is also the idea ARI, the group I lead, put at the center of its own frontier plan that we released last month.

That plan called for examiners who are on premises with access to most of the things that company employees themselves have. The analogy was to bank examiners. Dario reaches for the same analogy. Today, for many large banks, the Federal Reserve requires bank examiners who are on site full time. They can attend meetings, demand information, and serve as an early warning system for banks that might pose a risk to the financial health of the country and maybe the world.

Bank regulators have worked through some of the issues that such an idea often raises, such as the fear that the examiners might be captured by the banks they oversee, or that their presence would somehow impede the banks' operations. 

Yesterday, @anton_d_leicht, one of the most astute commentators on AI policy, had a related proposal that would have private organizations like METR, Apollo, or Transluce perform that function. That is a sensible approach, at least in the interim, it seems to me. Dario's version is like Anton's in this respect. The examiners at Anthropic will be third parties like METR, not the government. That is the right first step. Government examiners remain a possible solution if the private ecosystem proves incapable of scaling to the task.

In any event, now that Dario has proposed it and is actually adopting this idea for Anthropic, it is clear that the time has come to make this a central part of frontier governance. Simply testing models that are going to be released to the consuming public is inadequate. The OpenAI–Hugging Face incident showed us that. There are models used internally by the companies that could pose serious safety risks to the broader public.

Internal examiners who can flag these issues early for possible government questioning, if not intervention, are essential.

We need broader, entity-based regulation if we are to ensure that AI goes well. It is my sincere hope that other companies will voluntarily adopt the approach Anthropic is taking, and that all of us work to bolster the funding and capability of the organizations doing evaluations. They are now carrying far more weight than their budgets suggest, and that is the next problem to fix.

Revolut disclosed that it complied with a fraudulent government request using a spoofed official email and valid credentials, exposing PII belonging to a group of customers.

The leaked data reportedly includes passports/driving licences, verification selfies, names, DOBs, occupations, home addresses, emails, phone numbers, IBANs, account statements and full transaction histories, including Bitcoin activity.

No customer funds were reportedly lost and Revolut says its systems were not hacked. 

The company has notified affected users and regulators and blocked the source.

Social-engineering attacks are on the rise, with attackers increasingly exploiting human trust and weak verification processes rather than technical vulnerabilities.

text:
Ambition is the Bottleneck now

@tarstarr (Tara Seshan) (@OpenAI , product lead for Codex and ChatGPT Work), interviewed by @lennysan  (Lenny Rachitsky), Lenny's Podcast

The easy work is now trivially easy and the hard work is easy, so what separates people and companies is the ambition behind what they are willing to attempt. Seshan runs Codex and ChatGPT Work at OpenAI. Her operating rules follow from that: build for models 2 to 3 months out, ship prototypes instead of documents, and treat raising other people's ambition as part of the job.

1. Steering Over Rowing. Agents do the rowing and people steer, and the steering keeps moving up a level. It used to be a line of code, then pressing tab, then a goal, and Seshan expects it to keep climbing. Picking the direction stays human, and she describes it as a positive determinism about what you want the world to look like rather than a readout from data. Her next problem is multiplayer: people at OpenAI were sending each other screenshots of their Codex threads in Slack, which is a poor way to work with agents together.

2. The Ambition Bottleneck. "Not only are we able to be more ambitious, we almost need to be more ambitious." The people Seshan sees getting the most out of AI use it to widen the set of things they can do at all, beyond automating rote tasks. The old unicorn hire was the product thinker who could also engineer and design, because that person removed the translation layers between functions, and everyone has that now. The constraint moved from what you can execute to what you can imagine, and expanding your own thinking is the hard part.

3. Raising Other People's Ambition. Seshan cites Tyler Cowen: people underrate walking up to someone and asking whether they could do the more ambitious version, or do it faster, or do it at 10x the scale. She treats that as a large part of the PM job, so when someone proposes a timeline or a v1 scope, the response is to ask whether the ceiling is higher. Her evidence is Patrick Collison's list of projects executed at unreasonable speed, all of which happened before these tools existed. If those were possible then, the count should be climbing fast now.

4. The Two To Three Month Rule. "You fail if you build for where the models are now. You fail if you build for where you think the models will be in a year. Both outcomes are equally wrong." Seshan builds for capability 2 to 3 months out, which only works if product stays tied to what research has on its roadmap. The discipline is putting model capability at the center and getting your own product constructs out of the model's way. She quotes Kevin Weil's line that this is the worst the models will ever be, and says it is absurd that it keeps being true.

5. Empirical Over Academic. At Stripe, payments rewarded rigor: you could reason through a competitor's next move, and failing to do that showed up as carelessness. Seshan found AI markets too emergent for that, so being prolific beats being theoretical, and the switch felt jarring enough that she wondered whether she was skipping her due diligence. What replaced the long reasoning doc is sharpening one hypothesis to a point, testing it, and feeding the result back in. She borrows Shishir Mehrotra's term for it, the eigenquestion: the one thing that determines whether the product works.

6. Founders, Plural. OpenAI is founders led rather than founder led, with very little top-down direction and almost no distance between a product lead and the market. Seshan expected a treasure trove of secret strategy, the way a new hire at Stripe gets handed the payments bible, and there was none. Every view about how the world should work becomes public product or public messaging quickly. She credits the Codex turnaround to that structure: people who noticed something should be better went and built it without asking.

7. Three Questions That Run Product. OpenAI operates on three internal questions. "Is this maximally accelerated?" came from Nick Turley and covers speed. "Are you mainlining it yet?" is the one Seshan and Andrew Ambrosino ask their team, and it means using the product all day every day to do your actual job. The third asks whether the team is being as ambitious as possible, which covers scope.

8. Knowledge Work Isn't Code. Coding is output-verifiable: run the tests and you can trust the answer. Seshan says knowledge work breaks that, because you cannot look at the finished deck, see 90%, and believe it without inspecting the process, the inputs, and the reasoning. So the product has to show in-progress work, citations, and chain of thought, and take the user along to the answer. It also puts the thread format itself in question, since threads were built for coding.

9. Writing As Thinking. Seshan splits writing at work in two and treats the halves oppositely. Writing as reporting covers status updates and launch plans, and she hands all of it to the model. Writing as thinking covers the brief that argues for a product or a strategy, and she never automates it: "I start myself and I end myself," using AI in the middle only to pull data or push back on her ideas. The same rule governs her meetings, where she prepares for the total time everyone will collectively spend in the room.

10. Mocks, Not Docs. A long document stopped being proof that you thought about something, because anyone can now generate a long document that proves the opposite. Seshan still writes hundreds of docs, and she writes them for herself. What she circulates is a prototype people can try, or better, an A/B result with a recommendation attached. She calls this the biggest personal change of the era.

11. The 70 Percent Doc. Take a document to 70% and let the people whose buy-in you need carry it to 100%. Seshan got the rule from an old manager and still runs it. A perfectly polished idea repels new ideas, which bounce off it, while something with rough edges invites people to work on it with you. At Stripe she used this to open new product areas, shopping a brief around and letting each person attack it before taking it to the next.

12. Product Marketing Fit. Seshan spent time at Sutter Hill to learn whether product market fit is luck or a playbook, and came away convinced it is a playbook. What surprised her most was how badly she had underrated product marketing fit, having treated PMM as glue between functions. Mike Speiser tests the narrative before the product exists: pitch 100 people, refine the positioning until the story lands, then commit to a product shape. Done well, that work can decide whether the company succeeds.

text:
The information today art. 

Are you the one to break the cycle.

Conspiracy or product of attention 🤔 

Why is it so easy to look outward and find what is wrong?

Another person.
Another community.
Another country.
Another way of living.

Pointing outward can feel easier than looking inward, because inward is where responsibility begins.

It is easy to study another person's failures and overlook our own habits. Easy to criticize another country while ignoring the wounds in our own community. Easy to speak about what others should change while neglecting the small piece of the world actually within our reach.

Maybe it is time for a different kind of attention.

Not blindness.
Not pretending problems do not exist.
Not abandoning discernment.

Simply changing where we place the weight of our energy.

Before asking what is wrong with them, ask:

What can I improve in myself?

What can I strengthen in my family?

What can I build in my community?

What can I contribute instead of merely criticize?

And when we do look beyond our own walls, perhaps we could become students instead of judges.

Look for what another person does well.

Look for what another culture has learned.

Look for what another country has built that might be worth understanding, adapting, or appreciating.

Because flaws are cheap discoveries.

Look long enough at any human being, institution, community, nation—or mirror—and you will find cracks.

That proves very little.

The more interesting question is what we choose to build once we see them.

Criticism may identify the broken stone.

Wisdom asks whether it can become part of a bridge.

Maybe we have spent enough time pointing.

Look inward.
Build nearby.
Learn outward.
Carry forward what is good.

Then move on.

A Mind Muse

text:
Without commenting on the correctness of this claim, I want to briefly say a few words about what it would mean in practice.

Chess is supportable as a hobby in part because one can pick up the rules of chess in an afternoon. While one can't quickly play at a high level, it is relatively easy to appreciate the game, and have fun at it.

Research math is not like this. Over the last decades we have made incredible progress understanding basic concepts (number, shape, etc.) but the edifice we have built to do so requires an incredible time investment. Learning the ideas that go into proving, or understanding the proof of, basic statements like Fermat's last theorem requires years of institutional support.

It's possible that soon, AI will be able to do work at this level; despite recent successes, this isn't the case yet. But even if it can do this, why would it? Without people who care about these deep but fundamental ideas, who will ask it to? Perhaps it might on its own, or a person asking it to "do some cool math" might elicit a similarly deep idea, but who would understand it, if doing so requires years of unsupported work?

In practice, turning pure math into a hobby means the end of pure math, and the end of people who understand basic mathematical concepts at a deep level. Whether this is something we want is something we'll have to decide together.

We’ve updated the map of $EMBER

Team members reached out with more context on a wallet that created a cluster:

Wallet GZjYfG is a reward distributor

It's now labeled and hidden

***

This context wasn’t available onchain

Ember’s flywheel mechanism is not standard

Rewards are sent from a regular EOA controlled offchain, rather than through a contract that can be identified automatically. From an onchain perspective, GZjYfG looks like a wallet sending tokens to other holders.

The connections were correct.

The missing piece was Ember’s offchain setup

***

This highlights a few misconceptions about Bubblemaps:

1. A cluster does NOT mean a scam

Clusters show connections between holders, which can (sometimes) have legitimate explanations. The issue is obfuscation, not concentration.

2. Label is context

Bubblemaps shows onchain connections. A missing label never change the underlying data, but it can provide context to help understand what those connections mean

3. Labeling should be a shared effort

We label as much as we can (1B+ labels), but we can’t reverse-engineer every custom mechanism across every chain.

Projects know their infra better than anyone: contracts, treasuries, fees, reward systems, etc. And they shouldn’t want us guessing. That’s why anyone can submit labels directly through Bubblemaps:

https://t.co/YSixYQIsOO

***

Thanks for reading!

LVMH-backed PE firm L Catterton acquired a majority stake in HYROX, valuing the fitness race at ~$700m.

In 2026, HYROX is projected to make $270m (2x sales in 2025) across 121 events in 34 countries. 

That includes 1.5 million participants paying $80 to $160 to compete (with another 1.4 million spectators paying $10 to $25 to watch).

All while doing zero paid advertising. 

HYROX was founded in 2017 by Christian Toetzke (athletic events entrepreneur) and Moritz Fürste (an Olympic gold-medal winning German field hockey player).

They set out to make a standardized indoor race that millions of gymgoers could pick up mixing cardio and weights.

The race: 1km followed by a functional workout (eg. burpees, sled push) repeated 8 times.

The pair went gym-to-gym to get the race off the ground. By 2019, there were only 3,000 participants (grown 500x since). 

The entire thing almost went bankrupt during COVID. In 2022, they sold a majority stake to a Swiss sports marketing company backed by Chinese conglomerate Dalian Wanda.

Toetzke (CEO) and Fürste teamed up with L Catterton to buy it back and go all in om expansion, including trying to get HYROX into the Olympic Games over the next decade.

OpenAI just launched the most human voice AI we’ve ever seen.

It listens and speaks at the same time, handles interruptions and can even take phone calls.

It’s called GPT-Live-1.

Here’s how it works ↓

1. Traditional voice agents use three separate systems:

Speech-to-text → AI model → text-to-speech

Every handoff adds delay and loses context.

GPT-Live-1 handles listening and speaking inside one model, so the conversation keeps moving.

2. You can interrupt it mid-sentence.

Laugh. Hesitate. Change your question. Speak to someone nearby.

It understands what happened and continues naturally.

In early tests, Speak says it cut unwanted interruptions by almost 80% compared with turn-based systems.

3. Developers can control:

• Tone
• Pace
• Speaking style
• Custom voices

It also handles background noise, long silences and longer conversations without constantly interrupting or narrating every step.

4. The voice model does not have to do everything itself.

It can keep the conversation moving while passing deeper reasoning and tool calls to GPT-6 Astra or another model.

That means phone agents can book restaurants, update orders or solve support problems.

5. On OpenAI’s tests, GPT-Live-1 improved Full Duplex Bench performance by 30 points over GPT-Realtime-2.1.

One healthcare company says it removed 23,000 lines of code from its old voice stack.

Voice agents can finally behave like a conversation, not a phone menu.

US corporates have raised €149 billion, or $173 billion, in European bonds so far in 2026, the 2nd-highest annual total on record.

At this pace, US firms are set to borrow a record €225 billion, or $261 billion, this year.

This comes as heavy AI-related borrowing from Big Tech has crowded the US Dollar bond market, leaving other issuers facing worse pricing and less room to raise debt domestically.

Euro-denominated debt is also cheaper to service for high-grade borrowers than US Dollar debt, a key advantage for global companies earning revenue in Euros.

US firms are increasingly looking abroad for financing as the US market can no longer easily absorb the debt wave.
