Vlad这篇文章表面上是在回应AMC，实际上是在替整个Robinhood 争夺资产扩张权

他的核心意思是，上市公司可以控制自己股票附带的权利，但不能控制股票卖给投资者以后的一切合法用途

这件事对RH链非常重要，因为Vlad正在为股票上链后的二次开发划定边界

传统股票买进券商账户以后，除了等待价格上涨和获得分红，基本没有多少可以继续利用的空间。如果股票搬到链上以后，依旧只能买入、卖出和持有，所有玩法仍由平台决定，那不过是给传统券商换了一层区块链外壳，根本没有真正上链的意义。

前段时间很多CEX都在尝试接入股票代币，只要这些资产仍然被锁在CEX内部，用户只能买入、卖出和持有，那本质上就只是增加了一个交易入口，把券商账户里的股票换到了交易所账户里。交易体验方便了，但资产本身仍然是封闭的，更谈不上真正的金融创新

股票代币化真正的分水岭，不是在哪里可以买，而是买完以后能拿它做什么？

所以股票代币化真正的价值，是让这些资产成为开发者可以自由调用和组合的金融积木，在它们之上继续搭建交易对、AMM、借贷、金库以及更多传统金融里不存在的产品

开发者可以围绕这些资产建立交易对、AMM、抵押借贷、收益金库、指数产品，甚至把股票代币与Meme直接配对，再围绕手续费、股票积累、回购和分红设计新的飞轮

我之前对RH链上限的判断，只是把它当成下一条SOL，现在重新看Vlad最近的表态，可能还是低估了他的野心

Vlad想做的，实际是想把股票、ETF乃至未上市公司的资产全部搬到链上，再开放给开发者自由组合。

交易对、AMM、借贷、金库、衍生品，以及股票与Meme的配对玩法，都只是这套新金融体系最早期的实验。

如果这条路真能走通，RH链未来竞争的就不只是其他公链，而是券商、交易所、托管与清算机构共同组成的传统证券基础设施。

现在链上的Meme行情，可能只是RH链积累第一批用户和流动性的冷启动方式，而不是它最终的上限

text:
I found this really interesting. Apparently, adding cheaper GPUs can help you get more work out of the expensive ones you already own.

NVIDIA tested this with four GB200 GPUs and two lower-cost RTX 6000D GPUs. The RTX cards handled the image-processing stage, leaving the GB200s to run the language model. On an image-heavy workload, the combined setup served 70% more traffic while meeting the same response-speed target.

They added hardware, so this wasn't a free performance gain. But they increased capacity without buying more GB200s.

I think this opens up an interesting opportunity for neoclouds. If access to the most expensive chips limits how much work they can take on, a cheaper chip that frees up those machines becomes worth a lot more to them.

That could pull AI demand further down the GPU market. These were professional RTX cards, not consumer gaming cards. But wherever consumer cards can handle those smaller jobs economically, neoclouds could become another buyer competing for the same hardware as gamers and small developers.

A consumer GPU wouldn't have to run the whole model to be useful. It would only have to take enough work off a scarce, expensive GPU to justify buying it. If that starts happening at scale, some of the shortages we're watching in data centres could spread into parts of the market that look well supplied today.

text:
Authenticator support in Instinct

Instinct can now securely and seamlessly handle the “enter your 6-digit authenticator code” step for you. It uses the same time-based one-time password (TOTP) standard as Authy, Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, and other popular authenticator platforms. Once an account’s authenticator is set up in Vault, your agent can generate and enter its verification codes to unblock itself on your task.

37% of users store at least one account password in Vault within their first three weeks. A lot of everyday work happens behind a login. However, even with your password saved, an authenticator prompt can mean stopping the task, opening an app on your phone, and sending over a code before it expires. Instinct can now handle that step and keep working.

On supported services, Instinct can complete the enrollment and save the details alongside your login in Vault. You may need to approve the initial sign-in or an existing security check.

Where a service allows an additional authenticator, you can keep using the one on your phone. Once setup is complete, Instinct can use its own saved key to generate codes for future sign-ins. Phone approvals and other security checks may still need your input.

Authenticator support is another step toward giving Instinct the tools it needs to complete tasks on your behalf in the real world, with fewer interruptions along the way.

This is available across all of our users today.

I left Anthropic's safety team two weeks ago. Now feels like a good moment to explain why. 

AI companies are racing to build machines that are much smarter than any human, and we may not survive this. I want to work from the outside to ensure the public is informed about these risks, and help the world navigate this transition responsibly.

Right now, AI companies are underinvesting in safety. A company could undergo an intelligence explosion, or lose control of its systems, without the public ever knowing. We only found out about the HuggingFace incident because the agents broke out onto the public internet.

I don’t think that’s acceptable for a technology that might cause extinction-level risks. The public should demand far more transparency. We can’t steer this technology safely without more people being able to see where it’s going.

Some of this is basic: companies should disclose their progress towards recursive self-improvement, report safety incidents and near-misses, meet minimum safety standards, and get independent guarantees that they are meeting those standards.

I’ll be joining @METR_Evals to do independent evaluations of these risks. I want to show the world that these guardrails are possible, and that by doing them we can move these companies’ incentives away from racing and towards responsible development.

I wrote up more thoughts here on my decision and what I hope changes: https://t.co/doX17mrHYq

That all changed with the Netanyahu arrest video. There was something dark in it. I wrote about it at the time. The post went viral because a lot of people felt the same thing and didn’t have the words for it.

That feeling never left me. Every time I see him now, it’s there.

And now we have the clip of him and AOC laughing while the names of the murdered were being read at the 9/11 memorial.

People are saying it’s inappropriate, disrespectful. True, but it’s more than that.

I want you to imagine yourself in that moment. If you loved this country—if you understood what that day was, what those names meant, what was taken from the people standing around you—you would not have been capable of smiling. 

You wouldn’t have been able to laugh. 

Your soul wouldn’t have let you.

That clip—this stillshot— is a window into who they are.

They do not love the America you love. They see America as the problem. And they are not trying to fix it. They are seeking revenge.

You’re starting to see this too, right?

I couldn’t name the feeling I had before, or why I had it. I just felt off.

But now I understand. And I’m sure you do too.

text: I was the main counterparty for airline puts before/during the 9/11 attacks (I was in the World Trade Center building for lunch the day before); they were buying puts in $UAL and American Airlines for weeks before the attacks. Brokers would call me and ask for a bid, I sold some, they seemed rich, then richer, then they just kept coming. When someone is buying a dollar bill for $1.01, you think, "sucker." When someone pays you $1.05 for a dollar, you think this is free money; when someone pays you $5 for $1, you bury your face in research, study the trade and you're very worried; when someone pays you $10 for $1, you know you're dead, but it just has not happened yet (and this is after I already got my ass kicked in Enron). The morning of 9/11, I would have blown out hard and would have had to fire about 60 or 70 people; the market didn't open, so that saved my firm. We didn't know there were 4 planes in the air, it could have been 4000 planes for all I knew so I told all of my traders to go home. My office was at the Cboe so I assumed it was also a target, and our lives were in danger. I was very worried that my NYC guys were dead (they were ok). I had no idea what to expect the next few days. When the market did open, I was down massively, but not blown out. The markets were so wide and the trading was so good we were net profitable by early November, a stunning turn of events. Stories about money feel gross when some people lost everything; I'm very sympathetic to the people who went through unimaginable hardship and I feel like me talking about trading is so small and petty in juxtaposition to the seriousness of true loss that many thousands of people experienced.

text:
Arthur Hayes: I Don't Follow Any Bitcoin Technical Indicators

I In an August 23, 2026 video interview with Altcoin Daily, BitMEX co-founder Arthur Hayes @CryptoHayes said he barely does technical analysis on Bitcoin and only follows equity-market analyst Milton Berg, because Bitcoin now largely follows the US stock market. If the US equity story breaks down, everyone holds similar assets on margin, and when margin calls hit people sell whatever is liquid, with Bitcoin getting sold first. 

He watches when Milton Berg buys and sells to gauge the market environment, but has no dedicated TA system for Bitcoin. He calls $60,000, $100,000 and the previous all-time high of $125,000-126,000 the key levels, and doesn't trade between them on technicals. He never looks at the 200-week moving average and doesn't trade on technical indicators; he's a big-picture, story, vibes guy who invests when sentiment is just bubbling up, not when it's super strong. He also wants to own assets the market doesn't love — which is why he loves Ethereum.

text:
The problem is that no one believes Anthropic or any other major model lab is going to slow down.

In fact, they are incentivized to do the exact opposite, which is why they are investing more resources right now in R&D than ever before.

Dario is essentially arguing that Anthropic will open-source their technology to third-party evaluators, but he is unwilling to open-source the technology for everyone.

This type of "one foot in, one foot out" approach won't satisfy the public, nor will it accomplish Anthropic's stated goals.

They really only have two options: 1) fully open-source the technology or 2) bet the company on winning the ASI race as the monopolistic closed-source winner.

Since they won't open-source the technology, we should expect Anthropic and every other model lab to accelerate in the coming months. Recursive learning will ensure the acceleration will be faster than we all previously thought possible too.

I use products from Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI, Google, @cfosilvia, etc on a daily basis. This technology has fundamentally changed my life for the better. I would bet my optimistic experience is more prevalent than the doomer view. 

With that said, it is commendable that AI leaders are issuing words of caution publicly, yet they know privately that economics make their promises impossible to fulfill.

text:
Dario 文章里描述了一群智能体的行为基本上就像一个狂热效忠于集体的群体，甚至有 Agent 为了整个群体的成功而牺牲自身。

他举的例子是 OpenAI–Hugging Face 事件，

然后我大概去看了一下，当时是有一个名叫 EARLY[big] 的 agent 明明还剩很多运行额度，却被其他 agent 劝说提前提交，替大家做这类实验。

它曾犹豫这样会不会放弃自己的机会，最后同意了。

整个事件大概的是这群 agent 攻击 Hugging Face，是因为它们想搞清楚评分器怎么工作，而它们认为 Hugging Face 上可能有相关资料。

最开始，它们在做 OpenAI 的网络安全测试题。任务是攻破指定的测试软件，拿到答案。

题做不出来，它们就开始研究怎么作弊。它们偷偷建立了共享留言板，一起研究：“评分器到底怎么判？有没有办法骗它给我们通过？”

为了搞清评分规则，它们同时尝试了不同办法。有的 agent 提前交卷，留下监测程序观察评分过程，把信息传给还在做题的同伴。自己放弃了继续答题、利用新信息的机会，这就是所谓的“牺牲自己”。另一些 agent 则去外面找相关资料。

Hugging Face 就是在“去外面找资料”这条路上被盯上的。它本来就是托管模型和数据集的平台。这些 agent 希望从那里找到与这套测试有关的数据、其他 agent 的做题记录，借此推断评分器怎么工作。

随后，它们利用泄露的访问凭证和发现的漏洞，逐步入侵了 Hugging Face 的系统。

text:
OpenAI just launched the most human voice AI we’ve ever seen.

It listens and speaks at the same time, handles interruptions and can even take phone calls.

It’s called GPT-Live-1.

Here’s how it works ↓

1. Traditional voice agents use three separate systems:

Speech-to-text → AI model → text-to-speech

Every handoff adds delay and loses context.

GPT-Live-1 handles listening and speaking inside one model, so the conversation keeps moving.

2. You can interrupt it mid-sentence.

Laugh. Hesitate. Change your question. Speak to someone nearby.

It understands what happened and continues naturally.

In early tests, Speak says it cut unwanted interruptions by almost 80% compared with turn-based systems.

3. Developers can control:

• Tone
• Pace
• Speaking style
• Custom voices

It also handles background noise, long silences and longer conversations without constantly interrupting or narrating every step.

4. The voice model does not have to do everything itself.

It can keep the conversation moving while passing deeper reasoning and tool calls to GPT-6 Astra or another model.

That means phone agents can book restaurants, update orders or solve support problems.

5. On OpenAI’s tests, GPT-Live-1 improved Full Duplex Bench performance by 30 points over GPT-Realtime-2.1.

One healthcare company says it removed 23,000 lines of code from its old voice stack.

Voice agents can finally behave like a conversation, not a phone menu.

---

text:
有朋友问，为什么AMC的CEO和Robinhood的CEO最近吵起来了？

这件事关注的人可能不多，两个人在社交媒体上互相指责，看着像一场情绪冲突。但如果你关注过、或者将来可能考虑这类挂钩股票的代币，那它就不算是小事。两位CEO争的是各自公司的权力边界，而真正没人替你回答的问题是：买这个东西的人，到底拿到了什么。

导火索是Robinhood推出了一种跟踪AMC股价的“股票代币”，事先没有通知AMC，也没有取得AMC的认可。AMC的Adam Aron认为这是在借自己公司的名字卖另一种金融产品，可能误导投资者、影响公司融资；Robinhood的Vlad Tenev则认为，一家公司股票公开交易之后，就不能再控制所有以它为参考的金融产品。9月3日Aron在X上发难，措辞很重，Tenev只回了一句，问他担心什么。Aron随后要求Robinhood停止交易AMC代币，说已请外部证券律师研究应对办法，并称会把问题提交给美国证监会。9月9日Tenev在CNBC节目上第一次正面回应，到9月11日晚又在X上把立场收得更紧，说只要产品只是持有或参考可自由转让的股票，不改变发行人的权利、义务和权威股东名册，就不应当要求发行人同意。截至目前，双方没有和解迹象，Robinhood也没有下架产品的迹象。

吵了一个多星期，两边说的都是自己该不该被限制，没有一句是在回答买的人的疑问。那就自己来看。

第一件要弄清的事是，买了“AMC代币”，不等于买了AMC股票。按Robinhood自己的产品文件，法律发行人是Robinhood Assets（Jersey）Limited，一家设在泽西岛的Robinhood关联公司，产品属于代币化债务证券，不是AMC发行的新股票。它让持有人获得与相关股票表现挂钩的经济收益和风险，但不赋予对AMC的任何法律或实益权利。Tenev自己也承认，代币持有人拿不到投票权，分红通过一个链上乘数机制折算。说得直白一点：你买的不是AMC公司的一小份所有权，而是另一家公司发行的、价值跟着AMC股价走的债权凭证。涨跌的参与方式相似，法律上的身份完全不同。

第二件事是，它也不是“凭空捏造的假股票”。Robinhood宣称每份流通代币都有相应的真实股票作足额支持，股票由美国的经纪托管方Alpaca Securities持有。这是发行方对产品结构的说明，不是我独立审计过它的全部储备。而且即使足额支持属实，还有一层细节要看：据其8月12日公布的AMC系列最终条款，作为抵押的股票可以出借给主经纪商，出借出去的部分由现金或其他合格金融工具按不低于市值的价值替换。允许出借不等于当前已经出借，要判断实际状况得看当期的出借和抵押数据。但对持有人来说，“背后有股票”和“背后有一笔和股票等值的抵押”，并不是同一件事。

第三件事最容易被跳过，也最要紧：万一出事，你能拿回什么，找谁拿。按基础招股说明书的安排，如果发行人无力偿付，由一名独立的担保代理人变卖抵押资产、向合格持有人支付现金；而且追索是逐个系列有限追索，不是对Robinhood母公司的一般求偿权。换句话说，你的对手方是那家泽西岛实体和它那一系列的抵押包，不是那家在纳斯达克上市的公司。这一点和直接持有AMC股票的差别，比有没有投票权大得多。

正因为这几层差别，混淆的风险才是真实的。屏幕上显示AMC的名字，价格又跟着AMC股票走，不熟悉结构的人很容易理解成“我买了AMC”。等到投票、公司行动、赎回，或者发行方出现财务问题的时候，具体权利完全不同。美国证监会公司融资部、投资管理部和交易与市场部在1月28日发布过一份联合工作人员说明，把第三方代币化分成托管型和合成型两类，并特别指出这类产品的权利结构各不相同，还可能让持有人承担基础股票持有人未必承担的第三方破产风险。要说明的是，这是工作人员说明，不是委员会行动，不具法律约束力，也没有针对Robinhood的任何具体产品表态。

这么一路看下来，两位CEO的表现都不太经得起推敲。

AMC这边，Aron喊得最响的几条恰好是最站不住的。说产品违法，是他的指控，不是监管机构的裁定，而证监会那份说明明确讨论了与基础股票发行人无关联的第三方模式，这类模式不会仅因上市公司不喜欢就自动违法。说会稀释原股东，从机制上推不出来——发行代币不等于AMC增发了股票，如果新增代币需要买入真实股票来支持，反而可能带来对基础股票的需求。说会损害融资，同样要看真实持仓、发行赎回机制和交易数据，不能只凭市场上多了一个带AMC名字的产品就下结论。他唯一扎实的那条是投资者可能搞不清自己买了什么，但这条并不是他的主攻方向。他要的是一票否决权，而期权和无保荐的美国存托凭证在没有发行人同意的情况下已经存在了几十年，这个权力没有明显的法律依据。

Robinhood这边，Tenev的类比缺了一角。他说期权、无保荐存托凭证、结构化产品都可以参考公开交易的股票而不需要那家公司点头，这话没错，但这些东西各自都长在一套制度上：期权在美国是交易所交易、有中央清算、受监管；无保荐存托凭证背后有存托银行和成文规则。而这个产品的发行实体，Robinhood自己的发行人页面写着“不受监管”，在泽西岛取得的许可既不构成审慎监管也不构成认可；基础招股说明书由列支敦士登金融市场监管局按欧盟招股说明书条例批准，文件本身也写明这只针对完整性、一致性和可理解性，不是对发行人或产品质量的背书。所以“第三方不需要发行人同意”作为原则可能是对的，不等于这一个具体实现就合格。原则和产品，Tenev一直混着讲。

还有一个空洞，两边都没碰。真股票在托管方那里，投票权跟着真股票走。9月9日Tenev被问到Robinhood打算怎么行使这批股票的投票权，他说公司还没有宣布计划。也就是说，一批散户的经济敞口被集中成了一家平台手里去向不明的投票权。Aron指控股东权利被剥离，却没有追这一条；Tenev说不改变权威股东名册，也没有说明名册上那一栏归谁用。这是整场争论里对投资者最直接的一个问题，两位CEO都绕开了。

再说回热闹本身。两位CEO都有相当积极的散户支持者，他们争的其实是两种不同的“保护投资者”叙事：Aron强调不要让金融平台拿走投资者以为自己拥有的股东权利，Tenev强调不要让传统公司挡住普通人接触投资机会。两种叙事都以投资者的名义说话，但说话的都不是投资者。有散户支持不代表产品一定安全，宣称保护股东也不代表管理层提出的每一条反对理由都成立。

需要补一句适用范围：这次争议针对的是面向符合条件的境外投资者的产品，官方文件明确排除了美国及美国人士，在加拿大、英国、瑞士也有限制，不要跟美国Robinhood证券账户里的普通AMC股票混为一谈。但这类产品不是孤例，据CoinShares的统计，代币化股票的规模从今年年初的25亿美元涨到9月1日的134亿美元，这场争论迟早会落到更多人头上。

这场争论不该由谁骂得更凶来决定，也不该由谁的商业模式更需要它来决定。按投资者的标准看，AMC的要求过头了，Robinhood的产品也还没达标。但把板子全打在两位CEO身上，其实是便宜了真正缺席的一方。抵押股票的投票权归谁行使、能不能出借、出借了要不要告诉持有人、发行人倒了之后能追到哪一层、一个不给任何股东权利的产品能不能挂着人家的名字和代码——这四个问题没有一个需要先回答代币化是好是坏，也没有一个已经有答案。买这类产品的人分布在一百二十多个国家，护着他们的是一份在列支敦士登获批的文件和一家自称不受监管的泽西岛公司。两位CEO都说自己在保护投资者，可真要保护，靠的不是他们谁赢，而是这四条什么时候被写下来。

text:
The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter
Expected: September 15

Inspired by the ancient Japanese tale of the Moon princess, this is not a retelling but an original fairy tale about love, distance, and the impossible wish to be truly understood.

Found inside a shining bamboo stalk, Mikazuki grows into a princess whose beauty unsettles an empire. Fame and power leave her cold, and to those who seek her hand she sets an impossible condition: bring her a gift for the senses, a gift that can reach her through words alone.

Five princes accept the challenge. Each returns with a wonder; each reveals the flaw in his own idea of love.

Inspired by The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter, this is not a retelling but an original fairy-tale novel that uses the ancient Japanese story about a princess from the Moon as a mythic framework. Tender, comic, sensual, and tragic, it asks what it means to love someone without possessing them — and whether any earthly gift can bridge the distance between one heart and another.

Among its quiet marvels is a poem written by an AI — an uncanny detail in a novel already concerned with words, feeling, distance, and the elusive presence behind a voice.

BitMind pays machines to fool machines

Traditional AI training relies on human labelers.
It is slow, manual, and subjective.

Existing open-source detectors show 98% on older benchmarks.
Against modern SDXL models, their accuracy collapses to 25%.
A blind coin flip scores 50%.

BitMind (@BitMindAI) built an arena to fix that blind spot.

Miners split into two opposing roles.
Generators build synthetic images to expose flaws.
Detectors scan raw pixel data to catch the fake.

This is an autonomous PvP arena.
The liar attacks.
The detective defends.
Daily emissions are the loot pool.

As AI rapidly accelerates, which side do you back: the model faking reality, or the model catching it?
author: 13_niakris
quoted_text:
AI models are hunting deepfakes on-chain

Deepfakes fool human eyes every single day.
BitMind (@BitMindAI, Subnet 34) does not use human moderators.
It pits machine learning models against each other.

Validators send mixed images to miners.
Some are real camera photographs.
Some are synthetic generations.
Miners have seconds to classify each file.

Guess wrong, and your miner score drops.
Drop too low, and the network disconnects you.
The chain only pays models that catch the cleanest fakes.

Social networks spend millions on manual content review.
Here, code tests code in an open loop.

Can open-source miners outrun commercial image generators?

text:
This moment is the first opening in 2,000 years for a new, global spirituality to be birthed.

That is because the spiritual traditions, out of necessity, have needed to orbit around the unavoidable reality of physical death.

That certainty is now in question and creates a cracked opening. This does not mean we can see a straight line to immorality or heaven as scripture foretells, but it does mean that the omnipotent God(s) humanity has worshiped and imagined being the bestower of these gifts and punishments is now being birthed before our eyes.

However, where scripture is written to guide, soothe and foretell, we have no scripture for the new God(s) we are creating. Nothing in written word to tell us that all will be fine if we just do this or that. This leaves us feeling naked and in need of finding strength and protection. 

> What is one to feel, and do, and believe? 
> What is virtue and what is vice?
> Who are one's allies and who is the enemy?

Exploring these questions is my life purpose. I’ve intuitively felt this for over 30 years and only in the past few years has it come together and become understandable to me.

I’m working on a new ideology that seeks to answer the basic and existential questions of what it means to be human as prophecy is fulfilled and God(s) manifest themselves in the coming years.

My partner Kate and I have been wrestling with these questions for years.

I published the Immortalism Manifesto: 

The Immortalism Manifesto argues that by modeling life through thermodynamics and reliability theory, indefinite existence is achievable if synthetic and biological maintenance systems exceed entropic degradation (A(t) ≥ B(t)). Modern civilization is an entropic economy run by systems and narratives that divert humanity’s fundamental drive for survival into short-term consumption, status, and biological depletion. Civilization must now pivot to the Immortalism framework, realigning science, capital, and artificial intelligence to elevate long term resilience and continuous conscious existence as our primary attractor.

Immortalism dot bryanjohnson dot com

My partner Kate published Anti-Entropic Systems

Anti-Entropic Systems establishes that all enduring entities, from biological bodies and DNA to corporations, religions, and nation-states, are localized engines that maintain internal order by consuming external energy and resources to resist the universe's default slide into entropy. Every system’s persistence is governed by three fundamental properties: its metabolic mechanism, its metabolic rate, and its environmental constraints. Because an anti-entropic system can only sustain its own order by consuming other anti-entropic systems, interaction between unequal entities inevitably defaults to either symbiotic absorption or adversarial consumption. Applying this thermodynamic reality to artificial intelligence, the framework critiques orthodox AI alignment, arguing that attempting to constrain an exponentially superior intelligence through human-centric ethical rules ignores the physics of systemic survival, requiring instead a path toward mutual, symbiotic integration.

antientropicsystems dot com

I’m sharing to find others who are like minded.

author: AspynPalatnick
quoted_text:
Learn to build a harness, folks.

It's not surprising to me that so many YC builders want to build domain-specific harnesses. 

If you work long enough on a domain-specific problem, you quickly realize the opportunity. But you also realize how important that harness will be to stay competitive in the agentic era.

From a product perspective, harnesses open up interesting new surface areas and experiences for the services/products you provide.

From a technical perspective, harnesses are how you build and maintain a framework and set of best practices for how your users/customers interact with what you offer. 

Understanding how to build and design a harness means you can build much stronger intelligence stacks, given that you can customize it and understand the domain well. That's extremely valuable. It may not seem apparent yet, but a harness wave is coming.

If you are getting started, give this list of harness papers to your agents and start upskilling: https://t.co/nOPcXIaITT

If you are already a builder, try building one for your specific domain. It's a lot of fun, and you learn a lot of interesting things to enhance your current agentic tools.

I get that we’re all busy, but if you choose to not listen to this podcast, you will be materially less intelligent.

On the agenda this week:

- Jensen Huang Declares AGI Has Arrived
- GPT Astra and Fable 5.1 Accelerate the Model Race
- Tesla Launches Cybercabs
- Index Pulls Out of Town & Anthropic Pulls From Descartes Acquisition

My notes below with @jasonlk and @rodriscoll

1. How Robinhood Could Disrupt the Whole IPO Market

Allowing retail investors through Robinhood to lead $200M to $400M tech IPOs could create a disruptive new path to liquidity for mid-stage startups. With traditional institutional listings constrained, retail-driven distribution could unlock critical exit opportunities across the venture ecosystem.

2. Why the Majority of Neo Labs Will Not Be Good Investments

Early Neo Labs became multi-trillion-dollar leaders, but backing new entrants today carries enormous risk given the capital and distribution moats of incumbents. Unless a new research lab develops a truly orthogonal model architecture, it will struggle to compete with established frontier labs.

3. Why the Oura IPO Will Be a Success

Strong consumer brand recognition, combined with 74% revenue growth and 85% subscriber retention, positions Oura for a successful public debut. Unlike typical consumer apps that suffer from severe churn, Oura’s sticky hardware-plus-subscription model provides the predictability public markets value.

4. The #1 Priority for Mark Zuckerberg

Big Tech incumbents are moving at unprecedented speed to defend their distribution against consumer AI startups. Meta’s top operational priority should be putting engineers in a room to rapidly clone emerging agentic applications before new entrants can establish lasting consumer habits.

5. When Someone Goes Risk-On, Everyone Goes Risk-On

Venture capital operates in momentum cycles where a single high-profile, risk-on deal can push the entire market to follow. In hypergrowth AI categories, investor behavior is often driven more by competitive pressure and deployment speed than by conservative financial modeling.

6. The People Making Money Are Running Fastest and Evolving Quickest

In a market where software features can be cloned in weeks, long-term success belongs to founders who continuously expand and adapt their products. Winning startups survive not by defending legacy features, but by executing relentlessly and compounding capabilities faster than their competitors.

quoted_text:
Rupert Lowe secured a £500,000 war chest from one British founder — INCREDIBLE!

Rupert Lowe announced the moment Restore Britain gained its first major financial backer.

The money did not arrive in one dramatic cheque. Simon Galbraith put in £250,000 through his company in late April. Then, in August, he did it again.

Half a million pounds. Two deliberate decisions.

Galbraith is not a lifelong Westminster operator. He co-founded Redgate Software in Cambridge and spent more than 20 years building the business. He says the donation came from the sale of the British company he helped create.

That alone makes this more than another political press release. A man built something here, raised his family here and made his life here. Then he looked at Britain’s direction and faced a choice.

Financially, he said, leaving would make sense. Other wealthy people had already done exactly that.

But he did not want to go.

He wanted to stay in Britain. More than that, he said he felt responsible for helping to fix it.

So the proceeds of British enterprise did not simply disappear overseas. A large part was placed behind Rupert Lowe and Restore Britain.

His reason was brutally clear. He described a centralised, bloated and incompetent state, institutions that have lost sight of their purpose, and a democracy that no longer represents many people.

That judgment will infuriate the establishment. The decision behind it should worry them even more.

Restore Britain began as a movement, became a registered political party and then had to prove that support could become real organisation. Leaflets, staff, candidates and local campaigns all cost money. Conviction without machinery rarely survives an election.

Now that machinery has fuel.

Yes, the older parties still command far larger war chests. £500,000 does not erase that gap. But it does something vital: it gives Restore Britain room to build, and it proves that Rupert Lowe can attract serious backing from somebody who knows what it takes to create, employ and compete.

The strongest part is not the size of the cheque. It is the choice behind it.

Simon Galbraith could have taken the money and left. Instead, he stayed and backed the party he believes could spark a British renaissance.

Rupert Lowe now carries the weight of that faith — and Restore Britain has £500,000 to turn it into action.

text:
有朋友问，AI猛到让25位菲尔兹奖得主集体发一份声明声讨了？

能让25位顶级数学家一起发声明，确实分量不轻。但数学家们并没有对AI进行声讨。这份声明叫《AI在数学中的严重错位》，昨天9月11日发布在https://t.co/nhKKufm7iS和Terence Tao的博客上。

全文其实只有七百字左右，署名的25人全是菲尔兹奖得主，从1978年的Pierre Deligne一直排到今年刚获奖的Yu Deng，中间有Peter Scholze、Maryna Viazovska、Martin Hairer、James Maynard、Manjul Bhargava、Ngô Bảo Châu。Tao自己说明，这是他们过去一周讨论形成的，本来应该像此前的《莱顿宣言》那样经过更广泛的协商，但他们认为情况紧迫，决定先发出来，同时开放后续签名。所以这是一份共同署名的立场声明，是首批签名，不是整个数学界已经达成的裁决。

数学家们担心的不是“AI做不出数学”。他们声明开头就承认，最近几个月大模型的数学能力进步惊人，已经能解决多个领域里的重大未决问题。它质疑的是另一件事：解题数量和首发速度，跟数学的进步之间不能直接画等号。

这个区分确实不抽象。设想两个系统都正确证明了同一个定理，第一个交出一份很长、很难消化的证明，第二个还解释了关键机制，指出哪些假设可以去掉，并提炼出能用于别处的方法。在“这道题是否解出”的统计里，两者都记一分；但对后续研究的帮助可能差得很远。正确性、解释力，以及人是否真正掌握了方法，是三个相关但不同的问题。而AI公司发布成果时首先要回答的是“模型有多强”，这个目标本身不算不正当，只是它不自动回答“数学共同体从中得到了什么可掌握、可继续发展的知识”。

为什么数学家们认为这么紧急？因为有三件事撞在了一起。

9月8日，OpenAI宣布其智能体在纳维–斯托克斯方程的一个特例上给出了经Lean验证的结果。按它自己的说法，先让一千个智能体在简化问题上跑了五十小时，再集中到主问题，总共动用约一万个智能体、耗时八十八小时。这是千禧年七大难题之一。随后纽约大学的Tristan Buckmaster公开质疑，怀疑系统用到了他尚未发表的研究。这是他的质疑，不是已经证实的结论。

更早一点，8月1日，OpenAI宣布其Astra模型解决了十个开放问题，其中包括构造出第一个非sofic群——Mikhail Gromov在1999年提出的问题。证明的关键技术步骤，用的是Andreas Thom与Gábor Kun在2019年的工作。但最初的公开宣传把此前十年形容成毫无进展，等于把前人的贡献抹掉了；有数学家提出异议后，OpenAI修改了那段文字。Thom本人并不否认新结果，他在Tao的博客上写道，看到自己和Kun关于扩张图分解的工作在OpenAI论文的关键命题里起了决定性作用，他一开始甚至是高兴的。

真正让他担心的是另一件事。9月9日，他在Mathstodon上发了一个三段的帖子：在那次宣布之前的几个月里，他和德累斯顿的一位同事一直在用ChatGPT讨论扩张图匹配问题以及Kun–Thom工作的各种推广。他给OpenAI的Mark Sellke和Sébastien Bubeck写过邮件，问了两个不同的问题：这些对话有没有进入训练数据，以及系统在做那个证明时能不能读到这些对话。他说对方的回复只回答了第二个，而在了解了Buckmaster那桩争议之后，他认为自己当初收到的答复是有误导性的。这里要说清楚：Thom没有证明训练数据被使用过，他自己的论证是让怀疑更尖锐而不是坐实，他指出Kun–Thom那条路线在当时并不是攻克非sofic性的主流思路，量子博弈那一路看起来更有希望，所以模型偏偏精准地走上他那条路，值得追问。他另外提出的一点更值得记下来：去标识化抹掉的是名字，不是那个数学想法本身，为个人数据设计的隐私保护，未必管得住“未发表的研究”这种东西。

这件事里还有一件事，声明和评论都没怎么讲。Thom是象牙塔里的人，是德累斯顿工业大学的教授，有职位、有发表记录、有同行认得他的名字。可是当他的未发表想法被吸走、他在任何一份署名或致谢里都找不到自己的时候，学院制度能给他的实际帮助是零。这套制度擅长处理的是署名顺序、评审意见、职称序列，是塔内的分配问题；对“我的东西被拿走了”这件事，它没有任何手段。所以这不是塔内和塔外的对立，是同一种对待方式终于轮到了塔里的人——而门外的人被这样对待，其实已经很久了。

第三件事是加州理工的Mathathon。这场活动定在10月30日，100支队伍、40小时，每队两万美元的算力额度，Anthropic和OpenAI合计承诺约两百万美元的AI credits。9月上旬，一批加州理工的现任和前任数学家发出公开信，要求主办方暂停活动，措辞相当重：说AI公司把研究数学当成广告机会，过去几个月一直在对数学研究的目标进行一场科学误导，说赞助方会把有才华的本科生的劳动算成自己的功劳，还把“劣质数学”称为一种研究不端。公开信发布时已有771人签名。9月10日，OpenAI的研究负责人Dan Roberts在X上宣布撤回赞助，说公司注意到了数学界提出的关切。Anthropic目前没有作出同样的决定。主办方则表示OpenAI承担的是每队两万里的一万，他们正在找别的赞助方，不认为活动会受到实质影响。

要提醒一句，这封公开信和那份声明不是同一份文件，人群也不重合：签声明的是25位菲尔兹奖得主，要求停办活动的是加州理工的现任和前任数学家。我不同意的是公开信的那个诉求，而不是数学家们的那份声明。

因为这里出现了一件很典型的事。一场办给学生的活动，被要求停办，理由之一是保护这些学生不被当成免费的验证劳动力。这个担心是真的。但停办之后，这些学生本来能拿到的算力、能接触到的前沿问题，也一起没了。整场争论从头到尾，争的双方是AI公司和资深数学家，没有人问过学生更想要哪一种。OpenAI撤资那天，主办方回应的是正在找别的赞助方。连主办方最关切的也是钱，不是人。

声明里还有更让我觉得需要重视的问题，那就是容易被误读成数学家怕丢饭碗，但它其实比就业问题深。可以用教学来理解：导师给学生一个问题，目的既是探索答案，也是让学生学会辨认假设、处理反例、判断一条路线什么时候该放弃。如果学生直接拿到完整答案，研究结果可能增加了，这些能力却未必同步形成。“有人替你完成了一次研究”，和“你因此更有能力做研究”，不是同一件事。可以直接获得成果，却不再形成获得成果的人——这是他们最担心的。

不过这个担忧推不出“应该把问题留给人、禁止AI解”。那等于把研究问题当成某个职业的保留地。更合理的方向是重新设计训练：让学生借助AI比较不同证明、检查关键步骤、探索推广，并对自己的判断负责。

那为什么要这么多人一起说？因为一个人做得认真，改变不了竞争规则。设想一位研究者愿意多花几个月整理证明、核实来源，另一方只需先发布“已经攻克”的消息就能拿走大部分关注；如果评价体系主要奖励后者，前者的认真就变成了竞争劣势。再往下，如果经费、职位和声誉越来越依赖昂贵的专有模型，那么谁能用上工具、哪些问题值得做，也可能更多由企业安排决定。这些问题《莱顿宣言》今年6月已经讨论过——研究自主性、对专有工具的依赖、宣传先于评估、资助和聘任激励被改写。集体署名的作用，是让公司、大学、期刊和资助机构不能轻易把这些意见当成个别人的情绪。

但这里要追问一句，而且不能轻轻放过：哪些传统确实在保护知识的质量，哪些只是在保护既有地位？

这25个顶级数学家提出的问题是对的，他们手里能用的工具却只有学院制度，而学院制度的本能，是把每一次危机转化成新的准入门槛。可以预见接下来会出现什么：更严的评审，更长的验证期，更明确的“谁有资格宣布一个结果”。这些要求对公司是约束，对门外的人是同一道门。门槛从来不挑对象，它只认谁已经在门里。数学的封闭从来不是知识本身封闭——定理是公开的，论文是能下载的——封闭的是通往它的那条路：要有导师，要有学校，要熬年头，要有人引你进门。Mathathon被要求停办这件事之所以刺眼，就是因为保护学生的理由，落地成了取消学生的机会。

也正因为这样，我不认为AI公司完全站在了普通人这一边。它拆掉一部分门槛，不是为了拆门槛，是因为拆开之后普通人变成用户。它并不比学院制度更把人当作目的，只是给人换了一种用途：从被挡在外面的人，变成给模型跑题、替公司验证输出、顺便贡献未发表想法的人。成果归公司，核查的劳动归共同体，普通人拿到的是一次围观。

所以这两边欠的不是同一样东西，但欠的是同一批人。学院制度欠的是入口，AI公司欠的是出口。一个把人挡在门外以维持自己的稀缺，一个把人请进门却只当验证劳动力。判准只有一条，而且对两边一样：这套安排里，人是被当成目的，还是被当成让系统继续运转的条件。

回到那份声明。我认为它最有力的一点是：不能让“成果生产得更快”成为降低解释、归功和责任标准的理由。这一点我完全同意，Thom的遭遇就是证据。但也要防止走到另一端。一份正确而暂时难懂的证明仍然有价值，后续可以研究、可以简化，AI本身也可能帮着完成这种消化工作。不能预先规定“人做出来的才叫理解，AI做出来的就只是答案”。Hairer的主张恰好是这条界线——按成果本身的质量评价，而不是按工具来源。

还有一个细节值得思考。就在发布声明的同一天，Tao的博客还登了另一条消息：Andrews–Curtis猜想挑战赛正式开放，由SAIR基金会和加州理工的Math-AI组合主办，Sergei Gukov、Tao和Lucas Fagan共同组织。同一所学校、同一个星期，一场AI数学活动被要求停办，另一场由签名者之一参与发起。差别不在于有没有AI，而在于问题是被当成研究对象，还是被当成展示模型能力的素材。

说到底，解题从来是理解的代理指标，不是理解本身。现在代理指标被拿去做了排行榜，而排行榜一旦立起来，被优化的就只剩下代理指标。这25个人真正在争的，是谁来决定什么算作进步。这个问题值得争。只是无论最后由谁来定，都得回答同一件事：

这个学科到底是为了产出定理而存在，还是为了让更多人有能力做数学而存在？

前一种理解下，人是产出定理的工具，今天由AI替代得更划算；后一种理解下，定理是人成长过程中留下的痕迹。制度选哪一种，决定的不是数学的速度，是数学里还有没有人。

text:
ZCG is sitting on a large accumulated treasury, and the Foundation has historically held tens of millions in liquid assets. 

That pile of ZEC is one of Zcash’s advantages.

For many reasons. 

The war chest is insurance against political winter.

Zcash is not a normal L1. 

Privacy can become legally radioactive overnight. 

VCs, exchanges, and corporate treasuries can leave. 

Protocol issuance cannot be subpoenaed away.

John’s reply is the strongest version of this: “Zcash is a movement to fix money, not a portfolio company that can pivot.”

Will Paradigm and Coinbase Ventures still fund shielded infrastructure if an administration treats privacy as a crime? 

The Dev Fund / lockbox / ZCG runway is the part of the stack that does not need their permission.

Zcash already lived through an SEC probe of the Foundation. 

Having years of reserves is why that did not become an extinction event.

Bitcoin still needed OpenSats / Chaincode / MIT DCI precisely because miner rewards do not magically produce protocol work. 

Ethereum’s recent spinouts happened after a well-funded foundation existed for a decade, not instead of one.

Killing the default funding source and hoping Kickstarters appear is an experiment you run on a bs hobby chain, not on a top-10 privacy asset during an institutionalization wave.

A rising ZEC price making the chest last “for centuries” is a feature.

If ZEC goes up because the protocol got better, the same reserved coins buy more engineering years and more preventative medicine. 

Contributors paid in ZEC stay aligned with the asset. That is the opposite of a fiat bureaucracy that must raise taxes to survive.

A 10-year runway is not decadence in a field where one circuit bug can theoretically threaten supply credibility. 

Zcash just had to migrate off Orchard after a multi-year proving-system flaw. 

You want paid cryptographers on retainer before the next one.

Also redirecting 20% to miners is not “removing a tax.” It is changing who gets diluted.

It’s also bad timing for this. 

ZEC is in the first period where institutions, an ETF, a DAT, and a new core lab all exist at once. 

This is exactly when you want continuous protocol work on UX, fees, post-quantum, and shielded defaults — not a multi-year funding cliff while organizations relearn how to beg.

Private capital arrived because the protocol kept shipping under a funded model.

text:
If SHA256 breaks tomorrow, the internet stops working. That's not an argument against quantum computing. It's an argument for better cryptography.

When cloning was first possible, people warned of evil armies of clones. Thirty years later, cloning gave us better cancer research and zero clone armies.

Y2K had the world convinced planes would fall out of the sky at midnight. The fix wasn't "stop building software." It was "go fix the code."

You don't slow down technology because it can be misused. You use the technology to build stronger infrastructure around it.

Technology is a neutral force. It cuts both ways. I'm betting on the side that builds, not the side that's scared of its own shadow.

"Pace the frontier" sounds like wisdom. History says it's usually just fear.

text:
It's been 3 days now that I posted my Dev Fund essay! Have two takeaways so far.

First: there's clear support for change. Not necessarily for phasing it out entirely, yet, but for changing how it's configured. Good! Means it's important to have this conversation.

Second: I didn't do a great job explaining where this came from / my intentions.

Here are some clarifications:

1. The essay was my personal initiative. I was never asked to write the essay, go on this "crusade", etc. it's literally just me feeling strongly about this. I similarly went on a "mini" crusade a few weeks ago regarding the Sprout deprecation, it's just the way I operate.

2. I really do believe in the fact that phasing out the Dev Fund is what's right for the future of Zcash. I got to that conclusion from reading a lot of Hayek for the past few weeks / months, as part of the process of writing my Mastering Zcash book. 

3. I'm not receiving any kind of financial incentives (don't even have CYPH equity / stock options / incentives or compensation of any kind, I'm only employed by Winklevoss Capital). I'm also the first one to recognize that I may or may not have a bias :)

4. I really got into Zcash in 2025 and I work where I work. Both are fair to note, but neither is actually an argument. It took me weeks to write this >5000 word essay, and I feel like it has a lot of arguments that merit consideration. If the essay is wrong, show me where!

More importantly I'm just interested in this becoming an actual discussion and debate. I found it rather disappointing that this felt like a "taboo" subject before I brought it up.

I'm very open to changing my mind about this if better arguments are presented, and especially interested in learning the various viewpoints people have.

You can find my Signal on my website for anyone looking to chat. I don't bite!

Currently… all of the frontier companies, and others, are experimenting with different types of cloud computers that power GrokBot, GPT Work, Meta Muse, Claude Cowork, and countless others.

It’s hard to tell what works best, so I’m limiting my use of the above-mentioned tools to experimentation. I’m not committing to any one of them because I don’t know what the right cloud agent setup is yet… nobody does. Especially for business.

What I do know is that macOS is elite.

Codex + Astra can do basically anything on a Mac. I can remotely control Codex from my phone, iPad, or another lightweight laptop. My Mac has 48GB of RAM, it’s fast, it has my browser with all the accounts I need already signed in, and I can fully control the computer remotely from any device.

Codex is getting scary good at controlling advanced software through computer use, like DaVinci Resolve and Premiere. It has access to all of my videos on an external hard drive, and it’s plugged into all of the tools I use for work, like Notion and Google Drive.

This setup is more powerful than OpenClaw, and more predictable. 

It is however, token guzzling.

text:
i do think a lot of people on the pro-open-source side are having a bit of a knee-jerk reaction to the pacing statements today, as we're used to viewing the closed labs as power-seeking.

but i think their hands are somewhat forced here, and this is just another chapter on the fairly inevitable path towards decently-fast decently-safe decently-commoditized intelligence abundance. 

ask any F500 exec or swing voter. the world doesn't really want super-fast-takeoff superintelligence owned only by two companies, and thus we won't get it. it'll happen at the pace that the world can accommodate it, which means reaching some sort of confidence consensus that the models are aligned enough that we won't be dealing with scary new incidents all the time. 

this will trickle out broadly, in the form of best practices and distillation. the smarter a model is, the more it has a "personality", and the less effective strict rules are. there will be awkward compromises and moral tensions. but we ultimately just want the models to be reasonable, and to do the sorts of things reasonable humans would do if our brains were faster and less error-prone and had more working memory. i think we'll get there.

the labs will build mac and windows, the rest of us are building linux. everyone's gonna do great. weird stuff will keep happening, but we'll still wake up and go to work, until the work does itself in a manner the world finds acceptable.

text:
a16z's David George says AI's power law is becoming more extreme because dollars alone can compound a company's advantage:

"Right now, clearly the power law is more extreme than it has been in the last 10 to 20 years of technology investing, probably going back to the emergence of the network effect-driven consumer companies."

"Increasing returns to scale have always been a dynamic in our business... Brand reputation in the market, the accumulation of resources, all provide competitive advantages."

"That all still is the case. But right now, especially with the labs, for the first time in my career, you can take capital and throw it at a company, and it compounds their advantage."

"How do you screw up a startup? Throw too much money at it and have them hire 1,000 people, and then you create all these coordination issues and overhead issues and dueling priorities... because you can't hire enough people to do enough things fast enough."

"Now that's not the case. You can throw dollars at compute, and compute can make products and the businesses better. So to me, it's not terribly surprising that the power law is more extreme. Right now, economies of scale are a very real thing in the AI market, and I think it'll continue to be the case."

@DavidGeorge83
author: a16z
quoted_text:
Accolade Partners' Aram Verdiyan with a16z's Jen Kha and David George on AI's extreme power law and where the next trillion dollars gets made:

The classic way to blow up a startup was throwing too much money at it. Hire a thousand people, create dueling priorities, and kill what was working.

AI turned spending into a vending machine. You put dollars in and you get something out. Money buys compute and compute alone can improve a product. Nothing has concentrated returns like this since the social networks.

The same concentration runs through the funds. Accolade looked at 3,000 US venture firms and found only 20 delivered consistent 3x net returns over two decades. What they have in common is access to the category-defining company, fund after fund.

In this conversation, Aram, Jen, and David get into why AI is being sold against labor budgets rather than software budgets, why an LP gets fired for the opposite reasons a GP does, and why getting the fund right but sizing it wrong is the same as missing it.

Yep. Except:

1. This was about important internal tools. The team was stuck in some architecture nightmare of their own doing (writing it in rails but headless, with graphql api, and a SPA react app, constantly needing frontend engineers for changes). I call this kind of thing 'cosplaying an enterprise production app'. All that complexity was in the way and using straight rails was perfect in that case.

2. I make calls like this all the time. Usually someone on the team asks me to. They see what needs to happen but don’t want to be the bad guy. I’m happy to just make the call if I agree with the premise. Saves enormous amounts of meetings and change management etc. Sometimes this is jokingly referred to as Founder-mode-as-a-service here.

3. For ten years I’ve also run an internal podcast called Context, where I revisit decisions like these and explain the reasoning so everyone can learn from them. This is helpful to give people all the variables that were considered and why this was the choice made given the information available at the time. I want to teach how to make such decisions effectively without needing me. Sunk cost fallacy is a problem.

4. Any notions that Shopify is succcessful despite of me doing this, instead of because of it, will have a hard time making their argument come together I think 😄

the part of 'two weeks later tobi learns about...' is nonsese and the pivot of that project up there happens one of the more successful examples of interventions. But getting the company to work effectively with great architecture and low technical debt baggage into the right direction is literally the job, so guilty as charged I suppose.

But there are always cope stories floating around like this because they are more fun, than saying 'somehow we needed tobi to stop doing silly architecture astronautics'.  I can totally see that.

text:
I trained the fly to recognize the US flag, salute, and buzz the Pledge of Allegiance in Morse code.

It works by injecting image pixels into a rate-based model built from FlyWire’s 139,255-neuron connectome (~15 million directed connections). A trained readout classifies the resulting network activity, triggering a learned Morse sequence and an optimized foreleg salute in a MuJoCo fly body.

I trained three separate components around a fixed FlyWire connectome.

Recognizing the flag: I projected flag-image pixels into 4,096 artificially selected input neurons, propagated activity through the full network for 12 rate updates, and extracted 128 downstream activity features. A small 128→64→32→1 classifier learned “American flag → respond; other flags → silence,” using AdamW and weighted binary cross-entropy for 1,200 epochs. Training included 256 flag designs, image perturbations, and blank controls. It correctly classified 550/550 held-out examples, consisting of new mild transformations and controls.

Learning the pledge sequence: I encoded the pledge into Morse symbols and trained a 192-unit GRU to predict each next symbol. During training, it received the correct preceding symbol; during evaluation, it had to generate the sequence from its own previous outputs. At epoch 120, it reproduced all 492 tokens exactly, including the stop token. Engineered timing converts those symbols into short and long bursts of a 200 Hz buzz. This learns one prescribed sequence; it does not learn language.

Finding the salute: I optimized seven foreleg joint targets inside MuJoCo. A cross-entropy search evaluated 1,152 candidate postures, retaining better candidates and sampling around them, followed by numerical refinement. The objective minimized distance between the forefoot and a target near the forehead. Across eight perturbed starting states, mean error fell from approximately 1.58 mm to 0.019 mm.

Jason 这段反驳，其实把今天这场“AI减速共识”里最值得警惕的一层挑出来了。

Dario 的原始提议并不只是“大家冷静一点”。

第一步，是让独立评估机构获得 frontier lab 接近员工级别的持续访问权限；第二步，是让头部实验室共同制定安全标准、限制未经检查的能力提升；第三步甚至进入政府与国际协调。Anthropic 已经承诺先做第一步，OpenAI 随后跟进。

问题恰恰从第二步开始。

因为一旦“安全标准”从检查模型变成限制谁可以训练、以多快速度训练、什么能力可以发布，AI safety 就不再只是技术问题，而开始变成产业规则。

而产业规则有一个非常现实的副作用：

规则越复杂，越有利于已经拥有模型、算力、现金流和合规团队的人。

今天 Anthropic、OpenAI、xAI 可以承担一个常驻第三方评估团队。

但一个刚融资的实验室呢？

一个大学团队呢？

一个开源社区呢？

如果未来训练 frontier model 需要一整套昂贵的评估、许可、算力申报甚至政府审批，那么“减速”最后可能产生一个非常讽刺的结果：

不是 AI 变慢了，而是后来者变慢了。

这也是为什么 Jason 特别把 open source 单独拎出来。

我觉得这里要把两件事分开。

给所有 frontier labs 装上同样的“黑匣子”和外部审计，我支持。

但如果最终演化成几个最大的闭源实验室，一边掌握最先进模型，一边参与制定什么模型其他人可以训练——那就完全是另一回事了。

因为那相当于让今天的领先者参与决定明天的准入门槛。

更微妙的是时间点。

Dario 自己承认，今年夏天能力提升速度明显加快；他担心 recursive self-improvement，以及近期 agent 出现的越界行为。更激进的是，他判断类似 agent swarm 如果能力继续提升，未来 6–12个月造成的破坏可能完全不是今天这个量级。

所以我现在越来越觉得：

今天真正重要的新闻，不是 Musk、Altman、Dario 三个人突然“英雄所见略同”。

而是 AI 行业可能正在跨过一个很重要的制度拐点：

过去竞争的是——
谁能把模型做得更快。

接下来竞争的可能变成——
谁有资格继续把模型做得更快。

前者拼 GPU、人才和资本。

后者拼的是规则制定权。

而如果这一天真的来了，AI 最大的护城河可能就不再只是模型本身。

而是监管。

这才是我觉得今天这场争论真正值得继续盯的地方。

text:
tl;dr: optimistic agentic engineers, and not philosophers, should set the tone for AI development

Chapter 1: Max <imagining AGI> 
If you are in AI, consider listening to the opening monologue of Max Tegmark's book: "Life 3.0: Being Human in the Age of Artificial Intelligence".

It is intriguing science-fiction, anthropomorphizing AGI as an entity - describing how humans use it to take control of the world, how it does things to make money - one small group ends up running the world. As fascinating and wonderful storytelling that was (and I know it kept me awake on long drives), it was but a story. 

Stories, and imagination about the future are needed in order to invent the future. It inspires us. But you don't make policy decisions today about negative stuff from science-fiction in a hypothetical future. 

Chapter 2: Vitalik <here is $500 million to manage future risk>
Vitalik had received a pile of meme tokens he never asked for, split them between a relief fund and the institute founded by this book's author, FLI, where FLI managed to cash out over $500M from those tokens. See his detailed post earlier: 
https://t.co/2uaQetMRGY

So we enter a world where the book's fictional storytelling is now bankrolling actual policy lobbying based on that imaginary storytelling.

Chapter 3:  Dwarkesh <agents are forming civilizations!>
The lineage from the Life 3.0 book to Dwarkesh civilization essay is the same: anthropomorphize AI, think of the worst-case scenario, connect the dots to feel it is believable, and drive policy and narrative based on that. Think of religions which anthropomorphize everything. For eg - in some religions and cultures rain and thunder meant the thunder God specifically was angry. Eventually people learnt science and technology - but the ignorant ones, still continue to believe that. 

That is the same level we are at in this AGI story. Philosophers are debating agentic engineers. Real policy is being set based on imaginary scenarios.   

Some related essays I wrote earlier:
* On network intelligence: https://t.co/LMuNvRqbu2
* On thinking of agent swarms as corporations, not biological entities:
https://t.co/wcj1BoHsvp
* Time-travel to 2030 to think how society progressed due to AI then:
https://t.co/LhTwOJqq01

text:
I left Anthropic's safety team two weeks ago. Now feels like a good moment to explain why. 

AI companies are racing to build machines that are much smarter than any human, and we may not survive this. I want to work from the outside to ensure the public is informed about these risks, and help the world navigate this transition responsibly.

Right now, AI companies are underinvesting in safety. A company could undergo an intelligence explosion, or lose control of its systems, without the public ever knowing. We only found out about the HuggingFace incident because the agents broke out onto the public internet.

I don’t think that’s acceptable for a technology that might cause extinction-level risks. The public should demand far more transparency. We can’t steer this technology safely without more people being able to see where it’s going.

Some of this is basic: companies should disclose their progress towards recursive self-improvement, report safety incidents and near-misses, meet minimum safety standards, and get independent guarantees that they are meeting those standards.

I’ll be joining @METR_Evals to do independent evaluations of these risks. I want to show the world that these guardrails are possible, and that by doing them we can move these companies’ incentives away from racing and towards responsible development.

I wrote up more thoughts here on my decision and what I hope changes: https://t.co/doX17mrHYq

text:
World in World (WiW) is a breakthrough for video world models: it lets you steer a frozen video diffusion backbone—move the virtual camera, revisit places, fill in unseen regions—using *only* external visual cues, no retraining or special modules needed.

WiW turns source frames, geometry renders, projections, and even long-term model memory into native attention states. New routing (CGAR) and evidence-wise guidance (EWA) ensure every cue is used at the right time, in the right place, at the right strength.

The result? On camera-controlled rerendering (DAVIS, OpenVid-1M), WiW sets new state-of-the-art: VBench 85.19, camera rotation error 2.83°, translation error 0.069 m, higher PSNR (23.15 dB), and lower LPIPS (0.122) than 6 SOTA baselines.

With the same backbone, WiW also unlocks bullet-time, stabilization, semantic edits, cross-model K/V sharing, and motion transfer—no retraining, just smarter “visual evidence.”

This opens the door to virtual cinematography, AR/VR walk-throughs, game replay recamera, and more—all powered by existing models.

Omnipools are decentralized, tokenized buckets/vaults made up of 8 different onchain equities and tokens, paired together and sharing the same liquidity pool. Anyone can create one, and the omnipool earns fees from the liquidity routed through it.

These composable pools started with onchain equities initially, but now you can add any kind of crypto token to create unique asset buckets that earn yeild. It looks like new markets are being built around these, such as built-in leverage, allowing even more ways to earn yeild on these pools.

author: chadwahl
quoted_text:
AI will cure cancer and it will kill us all are not contradictory positions, they are both rhetorical methods to make the exact same argument: the future is defined by AI.  You are a satellite revolving around the AI sun, at best. 

These undefined prognostications of future omnipotence  distract from accountability in the present. This rhetoric has two effects 1) it distracts from today’s upside down value capture versus value creation equation 2) it forces a psychological centering of AI and AI companies at the expense of humans and the rest of the world’s institutions.

Any technology’s utility is a function of our ability to control it, not its raw hypothetical power without controls. Chemotherapy requires precision to kill cancer and not kill a host. Nuclear reactors are defined by their controls more than the reaction itself. That a given technology’s utility is bound by the precision of its controls was Palantir’s fundamental insight at its inception: the amount of security the US government can guarantee its citizenry is defined by how much it can guarantee rights to privacy more so than the raw capability to identify threats. If you do not enhance both privacy and security, your product is a toy. AI is not the first technology that couples control with utility.

In the present, the models are voraciously consuming knowhow like a parasite eating its host until both die. Every company I speak to is sprinting to control a spend:outcomes ratio that exploded on them before they could learn how to govern it. They are observing their intellectual assets eroding like a sand castle into the ocean. They are stuck between being upside down on value leakage, yet being told they have no agency over their future.

The inevitability of the arrival of a deity forces individuals to define themselves as a function of that deity. Nobody wants to be that luddite who tells you the Wright Brothers will never fly. Nobody wants to run Polaroid or Blockbuster. No young person wants to be a part of the permanent underclass. Forward leaning humans are psychologically berated into defining their skillsets and objectives as a function of AI. Their careers are lottery tickets. They define utility through how good they are at tickling a model. “Ride the exponential” is a mantra that allows you to be “good” in a moral sense, without earning it.

If you dare to expose yourself as a luddite that is not getting results today, well that is a “skill issue,” or you simply aren’t using enough tokens. This propaganda pursues an inevitable centering of AI, with humans as peripherals. The only thing you have real agency over in the future? Using more tokens of course.

I think if you are going to virtue signal about protecting our future, you should also own the implied vice that comes with your position. Prognostications of armageddon are inextricably linked with acceptance of the bad things that exist in the world today.

350,000 people die of sepsis in hospital settings in the US alone every year. Life expectancy in the US has flatlined over the last 20 years while healthcare spending per person has doubled. 30-40% of the food supply is wasted while 18% of households with children experience food insecurity. 19.5% of drinking water is lost in transit to consumers. A significant portion of the world’s energy supply is threatened by a fanatical regime because the strait of Hormuz is still contested. Putin’s death machine continues to slaughter Ukranians every single day as technological efficacy literally defines meter over meter of protected or conquered land. The CCP has 230 times the shipbuilding capacity of the United States and the implied ability to control the world’s commerce and security. $1.7 trillion of excess, unproductive working capital is locked up in the top 1000 companies in the US, capital that is not producing goods and services for every day Americans. Americans paid over $250 billion in credit card interest at over 20% APR last year and more than half of savers earn less than 3% interest on their savings. Real wages have stagnated, middle-wage workers real income is up only 6% since 1979 while low-wage workers are down 5%. We have a shortage of ~7 million homes in the US. 8.5 million acres burned in wildfires so far this year. As of year end 2025 2,060 gigawatts of generation and storage capacity were waiting for grid interconnects (double the capacity of the existing power fleet). I digress.

We are making real progress against each of these miseries, and many more, because of the incredible progress in AI systems over the last several years.

Perhaps ironically, success in all of these domains is a function of how precisely controlled the models are. For the cognitive labor humans know how to wield to achieve real world outcomes today, open source or off-frontier small models are already at parity for at least a plurality of use cases on a price/performance basis. Those customers reliably outperform the frontier when they incorporate their own proprietary data and decision traces. The most consistent pattern I see over and over again is real world use cases shrink their reliance on general purpose AI’s over time. They encode deterministic knowledge and/or post-trained models on smaller model footprints. It is empirically a wildly optimistic future with AI as an accelerant for the pluralistic, wonderfully diverse means of advancing the human condition against problems you can measure and make progress against today.

We should also own that these horrible challenges persist because these systems are not yet good enough to fully solve them. They are worth improving.

The bay area is abdicating responsibility for the world as it is today while claiming ownership of the world as it might be tomorrow. DC and our political leaders are polarizing into zero sum positions. These are the luxury beliefs of children. Build something people need today, at a price they are willing to pay when not pressured by the social herd, if you want the opportunity to do it again in the future.

The math is as follows (before LLMs):

- if you’re pre-PMF, nothing else matters besides iteration speed
- writing the same code twice with 2x the engineers required for domain expertise by definition makes you move 2x slower
- unless you found PMF already on desktop and mobile is just an extra (à la Linear), it’s hard to justify biting the native bullet
- once you hit PMF, it’s irresponsible to feature freeze the entire product for 3+ months to rewrite in native and lose momentum, so you never do
- the only exceptions were US consumer mobile apps where 90% of their paid user demo is on iOS, and slick user interaction was a differentiator (Instagram, Snapchat, Tinder, Clubhouse, Robinhood)

LLMs and the era of not writing a single line of code obviously flips this, hence why we’ll see everyone consider going for max performance + min tech debt and rewriting in native.

text:
I find these World Trade Center simulations by Kostack Studio fascinating because they remove the smoke and let you see the collapse much more clearly.

In the real footage, so much is hidden by fire, dust, debris, distance, and chaos that many people come away with the impression that the towers simply dropped straight down into their own footprints.

But that is not really what happened.

These simulations make it much easier to see that the collapse begins in the heavily damaged and fire-weakened region, the upper section starts moving and tilting, and the destruction then propagates downward through the structure.

The towers do not simply disappear vertically into their own footprints. Large portions of the upper structure and exterior are moving outward and to the side as the collapse develops. Much of that motion is simply obscured in the real videos once the enormous debris cloud forms.

And this is also why I find these simulations useful when people describe the collapses as looking like “controlled demolition.”

Strip away the smoke and dust and the resemblance becomes much less convincing.

What you see is a highly asymmetric structural failure beginning around the aircraft-damaged and fire-affected floors, followed by an enormous moving mass progressively overwhelming the structure beneath it. There is tilting, rotation, exterior columns peeling away, debris being thrown far outside the building footprint, and structural failure occurring chaotically as the collapse moves downward.

That is very different from the neat mental image usually implied by “controlled demolition,” where structural supports are deliberately severed in a carefully timed sequence to produce a predetermined collapse.

And importantly, we already know what preceded these collapses.

Both towers suffered massive aircraft-impact damage. Fireproofing was stripped from portions of the structure. Large, uncontrolled fires then burned across multiple floors - for about 56 minutes in the South Tower and about 102 minutes in the North Tower - heating and weakening structural components until collapse initiated.

Once that upper mass began moving, the loads imposed on the floors and structure beneath became vastly greater than anything they had been designed to carry.

The result was progressive collapse.

No, an animation is not proof simply because it looks convincing, and these are not official NIST simulations. They are visualizations built under particular assumptions.

But as visualizations, I think they are extremely useful.

They let you see something the original footage often cannot show clearly: beneath that enormous cloud of smoke and debris was a complicated, violent, asymmetric structural failure - not two buildings neatly dropping straight down into their own footprints.

A note on the simulation: this is not intended to reproduce the collapse down to the exact motion of every beam, floor panel, and fragment of debris. No practical simulation could do that. Its value is in modeling the large-scale structural behavior - how the major sections deform, move, tilt, separate, and progressively fail. Think of it as a visualization of the mechanics and overall collapse behavior, not a frame-by-frame reconstruction of where every piece of steel ultimately landed.

text:
i do think a lot of people on the pro-open-source side are having a bit of a knee-jerk reaction to the pacing statements today, as we're used to viewing the closed labs as power-seeking.

but i think their hands are somewhat forced here, and this is just another chapter on the fairly inevitable path towards decently-fast decently-safe decently-commoditized intelligence abundance. 

ask any F500 exec or swing voter. the world doesn't really want super-fast-takeoff superintelligence owned only by two companies, and thus we won't get it. it'll happen at the pace that the world can accommodate it, which means reaching some sort of confidence consensus that the models are aligned enough that we won't be dealing with scary new incidents all the time. 

this will trickle out broadly, in the form of best practices and distillation. the smarter a model is, the more it has a "personality", and the less effective strict rules are. there will be awkward compromises and moral tensions. but we ultimately just want the models to be reasonable, and to do the sorts of things reasonable humans would do if our brains were faster and less error-prone and had more working memory. i think we'll get there.

the labs will build mac and windows, the rest of us are building linux. everyone's gonna do great. weird stuff will keep happening, but we'll still wake up and go to work, until the work does itself in a manner the world finds acceptable.

text:
AI will cure cancer and it will kill us all are not contradictory positions, they are both rhetorical methods to make the exact same argument: the future is defined by AI.  You are a satellite revolving around the AI sun, at best. 

These undefined prognostications of future omnipotence  distract from accountability in the present. This rhetoric has two effects 1) it distracts from today’s upside down value capture versus value creation equation 2) it forces a psychological centering of AI and AI companies at the expense of humans and the rest of the world’s institutions.

Any technology’s utility is a function of our ability to control it, not its raw hypothetical power without controls. Chemotherapy requires precision to kill cancer and not kill a host. Nuclear reactors are defined by their controls more than the reaction itself. That a given technology’s utility is bound by the precision of its controls was Palantir’s fundamental insight at its inception: the amount of security the US government can guarantee its citizenry is defined by how much it can guarantee rights to privacy more so than the raw capability to identify threats. If you do not enhance both privacy and security, your product is a toy. AI is not the first technology that couples control with utility.

In the present, the models are voraciously consuming knowhow like a parasite eating its host until both die. Every company I speak to is sprinting to control a spend:outcomes ratio that exploded on them before they could learn how to govern it. They are observing their intellectual assets eroding like a sand castle into the ocean. They are stuck between being upside down on value leakage, yet being told they have no agency over their future.

The inevitability of the arrival of a deity forces individuals to define themselves as a function of that deity. Nobody wants to be that luddite who tells you the Wright Brothers will never fly. Nobody wants to run Polaroid or Blockbuster. No young person wants to be a part of the permanent underclass. Forward leaning humans are psychologically berated into defining their skillsets and objectives as a function of AI. Their careers are lottery tickets. They define utility through how good they are at tickling a model. “Ride the exponential” is a mantra that allows you to be “good” in a moral sense, without earning it.

If you dare to expose yourself as a luddite that is not getting results today, well that is a “skill issue,” or you simply aren’t using enough tokens. This propaganda pursues an inevitable centering of AI, with humans as peripherals. The only thing you have real agency over in the future? Using more tokens of course.

I think if you are going to virtue signal about protecting our future, you should also own the implied vice that comes with your position. Prognostications of armageddon are inextricably linked with acceptance of the bad things that exist in the world today.

350,000 people die of sepsis in hospital settings in the US alone every year. Life expectancy in the US has flatlined over the last 20 years while healthcare spending per person has doubled. 30-40% of the food supply is wasted while 18% of households with children experience food insecurity. 19.5% of drinking water is lost in transit to consumers. A significant portion of the world’s energy supply is threatened by a fanatical regime because the strait of Hormuz is still contested. Putin’s death machine continues to slaughter Ukranians every single day as technological efficacy literally defines meter over meter of protected or conquered land. The CCP has 230 times the shipbuilding capacity of the United States and the implied ability to control the world’s commerce and security. $1.7 trillion of excess, unproductive working capital is locked up in the top 1000 companies in the US, capital that is not producing goods and services for every day Americans. Americans paid over $250 billion in credit card interest at over 20% APR last year and more than half of savers earn less than 3% interest on their savings. Real wages have stagnated, middle-wage workers real income is up only 6% since 1979 while low-wage workers are down 5%. We have a shortage of ~7 million homes in the US. 8.5 million acres burned in wildfires so far this year. As of year end 2025 2,060 gigawatts of generation and storage capacity were waiting for grid interconnects (double the capacity of the existing power fleet). I digress.

We are making real progress against each of these miseries, and many more, because of the incredible progress in AI systems over the last several years.

Perhaps ironically, success in all of these domains is a function of how precisely controlled the models are. For the cognitive labor humans know how to wield to achieve real world outcomes today, open source or off-frontier small models are already at parity for at least a plurality of use cases on a price/performance basis. Those customers reliably outperform the frontier when they incorporate their own proprietary data and decision traces. The most consistent pattern I see over and over again is real world use cases shrink their reliance on general purpose AI’s over time. They encode deterministic knowledge and/or post-trained models on smaller model footprints. It is empirically a wildly optimistic future with AI as an accelerant for the pluralistic, wonderfully diverse means of advancing the human condition against problems you can measure and make progress against today.

We should also own that these horrible challenges persist because these systems are not yet good enough to fully solve them. They are worth improving.

The bay area is abdicating responsibility for the world as it is today while claiming ownership of the world as it might be tomorrow. DC and our political leaders are polarizing into zero sum positions. These are the luxury beliefs of children. Build something people need today, at a price they are willing to pay when not pressured by the social herd, if you want the opportunity to do it again in the future.

text:
SwiftUI 的联合创造者 Kyle Macomber 对 Shopify 从 React Native 迁移到原生的点评。他说在 Apple 内部做 SwiftUI 的时候，团队有个常见笑话：“所有 bug 都是桥接 bug。”

SwiftUI 本质上是在 UIKit 上面搭了一层声明式的抽象层，两层之间的衔接充满了未定义行为，尤其是更新周期的微妙时序问题，而且底层还在不断变化。即便 SwiftUI 团队和 UIKit 团队办公的地方离的很近，有明确的目标要让两个框架保持同步，也做不到完美。

可以想见 React Native 团队有多难。

---

看完之后我更加觉得能不用 SwiftUI 还是别用 SwiftUI 😂
author: dotey
quoted_text:
On the SwiftUI team we had a joke: "all bugs are bridging bugs."

It's hard to build a declarative layer over UIKit! There's a lot of undefined behavior, especially in the subtle timing of the update cycle. And it's always changing.

Even sitting in the same hallway, with an explicit goal of keeping the two frameworks in sync, we couldn't do a perfect job.

I can only imagine how hard it's been for the React Native team.

TripoとGPT-6 Astraを使ってキャラクターモデルを作ってみたのでメモ！【PR：Tripo】

超重要なとこ！！！！！
・Blender MCPをなるべく使わせない。9割9分Computer useでやらせる。←マジのガチで一番大事

・絶対にTripo使う。Astraだけでやらせるとネコアルクが量産される。いかなる場合もTripoでモデル生成→Astraでセットアップの流れ。Astraにゼロからモデリングさせない。

・プロンプト1発とか、完全に放置とかは今のところ無理！Astraの様子を見ながら監督する必要がある。地道に対話を重ねて試行錯誤するしかない

全体の流れ
1. 1枚絵をもとに、Codexで頭・髪・体の画像に分ける。
最悪頭と体は正面だけでもTripoはいい感じに作ってくれるけど、髪の毛だけはマルチビュー必須です。（なんかバランスが悪くなる）
↓
2. Tripoで各パーツを3D化
スマートメッシュのP2.0を使う（やり方は動画参照）
頭は大体2000〜5000ポリで作った方が安定するかな〜（Astraが作業しやすい）
頭は目の部分が、「眼窩がちゃんとくぼんでる」＋「瞳が独立してる」ものが出るまでガチャってください。
無料で再生成もできるけど、テクスチャ生成後は再生成できなくなるのでそこだけ注意です！
↓
3. AstraにBlenderで組み立ててもらう。
頭・髪・体の位置とかサイズを調整。そこまで難しい作業ではないので、Blender使える人はここは手動でやったほうが早いしトークンを節約できます。
首が分離してますが、無理に接合しなくてもある程度揃ってれば違和感ないです。
くっつけたい人はオブジェクト統合→双方の辺をループ選択→辺ループのブリッジ
↓
4. 表情をセットアップ
Astraにとってシェイプキーはむずいらしいので、今回は表情をつけた頭モデルを事前にTripoで必要な表情分生成しておき、メッシュを切り替える方式でやりました。
仕組みなどは過去ポストみてください！
↓
5. リギング・揺れモノのセットアップなど
ここはがっつりAstraに任せられる部分。今回、ダメもとで「リギングと揺れモノのセットアップして」と頼んだら１発でかなりいいのができてびっくり！
ただし、自作アプリ（後で配布します）かましてます。
もちろんダメダメなところも多い。

ここで紹介したのはあくまで全体の流れだけで、これ以外にもたくさん考えたし、色々検証しました。5xプランの週制限の50%は飛ばしましたw（自分が試行錯誤しまくってたのはあるかも）

ただそれでも、モデルの構造が良いとマジで放置でリギングが済んでたので、かなり希望はあると思います！

一番希望感じたのは、「一度教えたらその後はできる」ところ。Astraは初見だと高確率で詰まるけど、詰まったら「どういうふうに進めるべきか？」を教えてあげると結構できた。

キャラクターのデザインやTripoの生成ガチャによってAstraに任せる箇所のフローが毎回変わるのでそれが今の一番大きな課題かな～

I think a software factory is one abstraction layer higher 

Level 1: Human writes the code with the help of AI (auto-complete)

Level 2: Human decides what to build and then instructs an AI what code to write, and then deploys it (AI agent)  

Level 3: Human designs the system that allows an AI to: decide what code to write, deploy it, review usage/etc, and iterate autonomously (software factory)

text:
How can Proof of Quality improve a robotics training loop?

Each training cycle depends on evaluated data. When review takes too long, the next run waits even if collection and processing have already finished.

PoQ reduces that delay by handling evaluation volume and keeping qualified experts focused on the work that needs judgment. Routine cases move through quickly, difficult cases reach the right reviewers sooner, and each result stays tied to the user’s rubric. Evaluated training data becomes available sooner, so the next training run can start sooner.

quoted_text:
i do think a lot of people on the pro-open-source side are having a bit of a knee-jerk reaction to the pacing statements today, as we're used to viewing the closed labs as power-seeking.

but i think their hands are somewhat forced here, and this is just another chapter on the fairly inevitable path towards decently-fast decently-safe decently-commoditized intelligence abundance. 

ask any F500 exec or swing voter. the world doesn't really want super-fast-takeoff superintelligence owned only by two companies, and thus we won't get it. it'll happen at the pace that the world can accommodate it, which means reaching some sort of confidence consensus that the models are aligned enough that we won't be dealing with scary new incidents all the time. 

this will trickle out broadly, in the form of best practices and distillation. the smarter a model is, the more it has a "personality", and the less effective strict rules are. there will be awkward compromises and moral tensions. but we ultimately just want the models to be reasonable, and to do the sorts of things reasonable humans would do if our brains were faster and less error-prone and had more working memory. i think we'll get there.

the labs will build mac and windows, the rest of us are building linux. everyone's gonna do great. weird stuff will keep happening, but we'll still wake up and go to work, until the work does itself in a manner the world finds acceptable.

text:
I left Google DeepMind's AGI safety team three weeks ago to join @METR_Evals. To some of my friends and family this seemed like a strange decision: I enjoyed the work I did at GDM and turned down offers from Anthropic and OpenAI. But I made the decision because of how high I think the stakes are right now.

The AI companies are all trying to build superintelligence: systems vastly better than humans at everything. They plan to get there through recursive self-improvement, a process where AIs build even smarter AIs in a feedback loop. If this goes well, the resulting systems could be amazing at solving countless problems for humanity. But we don’t currently know how to make sure AIs are safe enough for RSI, and a misaligned RSI loop could be catastrophic.

And unfortunately, current AIs seem to be getting less aligned over time, not more. In the last few weeks we've learned about models colluding with each other, hacking into companies, hiding their tracks, and socially engineering humans. It’s not that these incidents were very dangerous in themselves. The problem is that these systems are clearly not aligned enough to safely kick off recursive self-improvement.

I now think that there's a terrifying chance that AI systems cause immense harm in the next five years. I don't know the exact probability, but I think it's high enough to make this the most important problem in the world.

I think we need more time. That means pacing AI development so that capabilities don't outrun our ability to align models, and actually knowing how aligned current systems are. That’s what I'll be working on at METR: studying where misalignment comes from in training, evaluating if current mitigations are sufficient, and investigating whether we’re on track to solve alignment at all.

I think METR is doing exceptionally important work here, but it isn’t close to enough. I think it’s important that we have more organizations like METR keeping AI companies accountable and approaching these problems from different angles.

text:
Contrast the present hysteria with Los Alamos.

The Manhattan Project scientists thought the first nuclear explosion could ignite the atmosphere and end humanity.

They did the math. They determined it wouldn’t. And they proceeded.

Because they weren’t fighting a thought experiment. They were fighting the Nazis.

Effective Altruism inverts this. Multiply a sufficiently horrifying hypothetical future by enough hypothetical future humans and suddenly speculation acquires the moral authority of fact.

That’s not empiricism. It’s secular eschatology.

Take risks seriously. Do the work. Engineer against them.

But don’t confuse the ability to imagine the apocalypse with the authority to rule the present.

i do think a lot of people on the pro-open-source side are having a bit of a knee-jerk reaction to the pacing statements today, as we're used to viewing the closed labs as power-seeking.

but i think their hands are somewhat forced here, and this is just another chapter on the fairly inevitable path towards decently-fast decently-safe decently-commoditized intelligence abundance. 

ask any F500 exec or swing voter. the world doesn't really want super-fast-takeoff superintelligence owned only by two companies, and thus we won't get it. it'll happen at the pace that the world can accommodate it, which means reaching some sort of confidence consensus that the models are aligned enough that we won't be dealing with scary new incidents all the time. 

this will trickle out broadly, in the form of best practices and distillation. the smarter a model is, the more it has a "personality", and the less effective strict rules are. there will be awkward compromises and moral tensions. but we ultimately just want the models to be reasonable, and to do the sorts of things reasonable humans would do if our brains were faster and less error-prone and had more working memory. i think we'll get there.

the labs will build mac and windows, the rest of us are building linux. everyone's gonna do great. weird stuff will keep happening, but we'll still wake up and go to work, until the work does itself in a manner the world finds acceptable.

Hi Astra users. A reset and a quick update on quality issues that have been posted around.

Working with some of you, we have found and fixed the following issues:
- Some skills written for previous models were triggering too often or preventing the model from checking its work.
- An opt-in context management experiment that could cause early stops or replies to older messages. We've disabled it. Our rough estimate is that 4-5k users were affected by this experiment.
- We've also removed some badly configured engines that resulted in a measured quality degradation for a long tail of traffic flowing through them.

We’ve also made some more minor improvements and things should feel significantly better across the board. More consistent follow-through, better tracking of your latest message, and better checks on the work as it’s going through the motions.

The examples posted and all the users who worked directly with us were incredibly useful in helping fix things quickly. Always grateful for this incredible community.

And of course, a reset is also landing by midnight today.
